name: Classic-Style Test 5
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: The Regional Press Council has urged newspapers to stop printing photographs of accident victims without the consent of the victims' families. But several of the council's own members are editors whose papers have printed exactly such photographs in recent years. So the council's recommendation does not deserve to be taken seriously by anyone in the industry.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the media critic's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that printing photographs of accident victims might sometimes serve the public interest
treats the past conduct of some of a recommendation's authors as grounds for rejecting the recommendation itself
does not establish that the editors' papers printed such photographs after the council issued its recommendation
draws a conclusion about all newspapers from the conduct of a few editors
confuses the council's authority to recommend a practice with any authority it might have to enforce that practice
questions.explanation: Whether a recommendation is sound has nothing to do with whether the people making it have always followed it; (B) names this tu quoque flaw. (C) is tempting because the timing would matter to a charge of hypocrisy, but even a fresh act of hypocrisy would not show the recommendation is bad. (A) raises a point about the merits that would only help the critic, and (D) fails because the critic draws no conclusion about all newspapers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council's recommendation against printing accident-victim photos without family consent shouldn't be taken seriously.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some council members edit papers that have printed such photos.

breakdown.analysis: So what if some council members didn't practice what they preach? A recommendation is good or bad on its merits, not on the track record of the people making it. This is the tu quoque flaw, a kind of ad hominem: 'you do it too, so your advice is worthless.' It's a classic; know it. It's like ignoring your doctor's advice to quit smoking because your doctor smokes. We need an answer that says the critic dismisses advice because its givers don't follow it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a fair point about the merits. But the critic never touches the merits, and this point would only support the critic's side. Failing to consider a point that helps you isn't the flaw here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Printing such photos causes families pain, so it is never justified (ignoring that a photo might reveal a dangerous road design).

choices.note: CORRECT. That's exactly the move: the editors' own past conduct is used to dismiss what the council recommends. Hypocrisy in the messengers doesn't make the message wrong.

Tempting, because timing would matter if the question were whether the editors are hypocrites. But it isn't. Even if every photo ran the day after the recommendation, the editors' conduct still wouldn't show the recommendation is unsound. Fixing the timing wouldn't fix the argument.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Councillor Ames voted for the parking rule, and she was ticketed for illegal parking, so she's a hypocrite (when the ticket came years before the rule existed).

choices.note: The conclusion is about the council's recommendation, not about all newspapers. No generalization happens.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Three editors I know printed such photos, so every newspaper in the country does it.

choices.note: Enforcement never comes up. The critic doesn't argue that the council can't enforce its advice.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The council can't punish papers that ignore its guideline, so the guideline must be mistaken.

questions.stimulus: Forester: Many landowners believe that clearing all the dead wood from their woodlots makes the woods healthier. This belief is mistaken. Fallen logs shelter the salamanders and ground beetles that keep pest insects in check, and as the logs rot they return nutrients to the soil. Removing them, then, deprives the remaining trees of both protection and nourishment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the forester's argument?
choices: Clearing all of the dead wood from a woodlot does not make the woods healthier.
Removing fallen logs from a woodlot deprives the remaining trees of both protection and nourishment.
Fallen logs shelter animals that keep pest insects in check.
Landowners should leave all of the dead wood in their woodlots exactly where it falls.
Rotting logs return more nutrients to the soil than any other source does.
questions.explanation: The forester's point is that the landowners' belief is mistaken, which (A) restates: clearing all the dead wood doesn't make the woods healthier. (B) is tempting because it follows 'then,' but it is an intermediate conclusion that supports the rejection of the belief. (D) adds a recommendation the forester never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The belief that clearing all dead wood makes woods healthier is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Fallen logs shelter pest-eating salamanders and beetles; 2. rotting logs feed the soil; 3. so removing them costs trees protection and nourishment.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. 'This belief is mistaken' is the main point; the facts about logs explain why, and the 'then' sentence pulls those facts together into a sub-conclusion that in turn supports 'mistaken.' Watch out: the last sentence has a conclusion word, but it's a stepping stone. We need an answer that restates 'the belief is wrong.'

choices.note: CORRECT. 'This belief is mistaken' just means it's false that clearing all the dead wood makes woods healthier. Everything else in the stimulus supports this.

Tempting, because of the word 'then.' But this sentence is an intermediate conclusion: it's the reason the forester gives for calling the belief mistaken. It supports the main point rather than being it.
This is a premise, one of the reasons the belief is wrong. Premises are never the main conclusion.
Too strong, and it adds a recommendation. The forester says clearing everything doesn't help; that's not the same as telling landowners to leave every scrap of dead wood.
Unsupported superlative. The forester says rotting logs return nutrients, not that they're the biggest source.

questions.stimulus: Researchers tracked 400 adults who had just received a hepatitis vaccine. Those who slept at least seven hours a night during the following week had, according to blood tests taken a month later, substantially more antibodies against the virus than did those who slept less. The researchers concluded that getting adequate sleep after vaccination enhances the body's antibody response to the vaccine.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' argument?
choices: Some participants who slept more than nine hours a night produced fewer antibodies than did some participants who slept exactly seven hours.
The antibodies produced in response to the hepatitis vaccine decline gradually over a period of several years after vaccination.
Most adults sleep fewer than seven hours on at least some nights.
Producing antibodies is only one of several ways the immune system responds to a vaccine.
The participants who slept less were, on average, no older and no less healthy than those who slept more.
questions.explanation: The study shows only a correlation between sleep and antibody levels; older or less healthy people might both sleep less and respond more weakly. (E) rules out those alternative causes, so the sleep difference becomes the more likely explanation. (A) is tempting but compares people within the well-rested group and, if anything, muddies the link. (C) concerns how common short sleep is, which has no bearing on whether sleep causes the difference.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adequate sleep after vaccination boosts the antibody response.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a study, people who slept 7+ hours in the week after the vaccine made more antibodies than people who slept less.

breakdown.analysis: Is it the sleep, or something about the people who sleep less? Older people and sicker people often sleep worse, and they might make fewer antibodies regardless. That's a correlation dressed up as a cause. We need an answer that rules out a different difference between the two groups.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about sleep and antibodies. But it compares people inside the well-rested group, and 'some' vs. 'some' tells us almost nothing. If anything it slightly weakens a simple more-sleep-is-better story.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. How long antibodies last says nothing about whether sleep boosted how many were made.
So? How common short sleep is in the population doesn't bear on whether sleep causes a better response. It neither rules out a rival cause nor adds to the link.
Irrelevant. The conclusion is only about the antibody response, so other immune responses don't matter.

CORRECT. Age and general health are the obvious rival explanations: older or sicker people tend to sleep less and could also mount a weaker response. If the short sleepers weren't older or sicker, those rivals are gone, and sleep itself becomes the more likely cause.

questions.stimulus:
Ortega: The museum should reopen its long-closed east wing to display our textile collection. Visitors ask about the textiles more than anything else we own, and the wing has sat empty for twelve years.

Kim: Visitors certainly want to see the textiles. But the east wing's roof leaks badly, and repairing it would cost more than any exhibit there could recover. Reopening the wing makes no sense; the textiles should stay in storage until a new gallery is built.
questions.stem: Ortega and Kim disagree over whether
choices: visitors want to see the museum's textile collection
the museum should reopen its east wing to display the textile collection
the east wing's roof leaks badly enough that repairing it would be costly
the east wing has sat empty for twelve years
a museum should pay for building repairs out of the money its exhibits bring in
questions.explanation: Ortega says the east wing should be reopened for the textiles; Kim says it makes no sense and the textiles should stay in storage, so they disagree about (B). (A) is something both affirm, since Kim concedes visitors want to see the textiles. Ortega says nothing about the roof (C), and Kim says nothing about how long the wing has been empty (D).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ortega: reopen the east wing for the textiles, since visitors want them and the wing is empty; Kim: visitors want them, but the roof repair costs more than an exhibit could recover, so keep the textiles in storage.

breakdown.analysis: Where do they actually clash? Kim agrees visitors want the textiles, so that's common ground. The clash is the proposal itself: Ortega says reopen the wing, Kim says don't. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. We need the answer that both speakers take a side on, and opposite sides.

choices.note: Tempting because it's Ortega's main reason. But Kim explicitly agrees ('certainly want to see the textiles'). That's agreement, not disagreement.
CORRECT. Ortega: yes, reopen the wing for the textiles. Kim: no, keep them in storage. Clear yes vs. no.
Only Kim talks about the roof. Ortega never says whether it leaks, so we can't call it a disagreement.
Only Ortega mentions this, and Kim never disputes it.
Neither speaker states this as a rule. Kim only says the repair would cost more than an exhibit could recover, and Ortega says nothing about who pays.

questions.stimulus: For the past four months a volcano has been erupting mildly, and fine ash has fallen almost daily on a nearby farming village, coating roofs and fields. Yet the number of patients seeking treatment for coughing, wheezing, and other breathing problems at the village's only clinic has fallen sharply since the eruptions began.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Fine volcanic ash can irritate the lungs and throat even of people who have no previous history of breathing problems.
The clinic is the only medical facility within a full day's travel of the village.
Since the eruptions began, most of the village's residents have been staying with relatives outside the ashfall area.
The ash particles are small enough to stay in the air for hours.
Ash from mild eruptions is generally less irritating to the lungs than ash from major eruptions.
questions.explanation: If most residents have left the ash zone, there are far fewer people around to seek treatment, so the number of patients can fall even though the ash is harmful (C). (E) is tempting because it makes the ash sound milder, but 'less irritating than ash from major eruptions' is a comparison, not a reason for complaints to fall below their pre-eruption level. (A) and (D) only deepen the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Ash has been falling on the village daily, but fewer people are visiting the clinic for breathing problems.

breakdown.analysis: How can breathing complaints drop when the air is full of ash? Notice the stimulus counts patients, not the rate among residents. If the people aren't there, they can't show up at the clinic. We need an answer that explains why fewer patients would come in despite the ash.

choices.note: This makes the ash sound more dangerous, so we'd expect more patients. It deepens the paradox.
This makes it even stranger: if it's the only facility nearby, anyone with breathing trouble should be showing up there.
CORRECT. Most residents are gone. Fewer people in the village means fewer patients at the clinic, even if the ash is bad for the people who stayed.
Again, this makes the ash more harmful, since it stays in the air longer. It deepens the puzzle.

Tempting, because it softens the ash. But 'less irritating than big-eruption ash' is relative: mild ash can still be worse than no ash. It might explain a smaller rise, not a sharp fall below what the clinic saw before the eruptions.

questions.stimulus: Ralston Hardware sells two brands of interior paint, Mayfair and Tenly, at the same price per gallon. A gallon of Mayfair covers about 400 square feet of wall with one coat, whereas a gallon of Tenly covers only about 300 square feet. And in independent tests, a single coat of either brand fully hid the old color on most walls. So a Ralston customer who plans to give a large room one coat of paint ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: will probably be happier with how the finished walls look if Mayfair is used
will need fewer gallons of Mayfair than of Tenly to hide the old color completely on every wall in the room
will generally spend less money on paint for the job by choosing Mayfair rather than Tenly
would pay about the same total for paint whichever brand the customer chose
is more likely to find Mayfair than Tenly in stock in the desired color at a typical Ralston store
questions.explanation: Same price per gallon, but Mayfair covers a third more wall per gallon, and one coat of either usually hides the old color, so the job takes fewer gallons of Mayfair and therefore less money (C). (B) is the near-miss: fewer gallons is right, but the tests say one coat hid the old color on most walls, not every wall. (D) is the misreading that ignores coverage.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Mayfair and Tenly cost the same per gallon; 2. a gallon of Mayfair covers ~400 sq ft, Tenly ~300; 3. one coat of either hides the old color on most walls; 4. the customer wants one coat on a large room.

breakdown.analysis: This is a fill-in-the-blank, so treat it like a must-be-true: the blank has to follow from the facts. Put facts 1 and 2 together: same price, but Mayfair stretches farther. Fact 3 says one coat of either usually does the job, so you don't need extra Mayfair to make up for weaker hiding power. A big room means lots of square feet, and fewer gallons at the same price means less money. We need an answer about cost for the job, stated no more strongly than the facts allow.

choices.note: Satisfaction with the look is about quality and taste. The facts say only that both brands usually hide the old color in one coat. Unsupported.
Tempting: fewer gallons of Mayfair is right. But 'hide the old color completely on every wall' goes past the tests, which say one coat worked on most walls. One word ('every') sinks it.

CORRECT. Same price per gallon, more square feet per gallon, and one coat usually suffices. A large room needs fewer gallons of Mayfair, so the job costs less with Mayfair. 'Generally' keeps it modest enough to follow.
Tempting, because the price per gallon is the same. But the total depends on how many gallons you need, and Mayfair needs about a quarter fewer gallons for the same wall. This ignores fact 2.
Stock and color selection never come up. Right store, wrong topic.

questions.stimulus: Music teacher: Our school district wants more of its high school students to join the orchestra. Most students who join the high school orchestra took string lessons in the district's elementary schools, but the district eliminated those lessons last year to save money. So unless the elementary string lessons are restored, membership in the high school orchestra will decline in the coming years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the music teacher's argument?
choices: Most students who took elementary string lessons in the district went on to join the high school orchestra.
Restoring the lessons would cost less than other ways of recruiting orchestra members.
No student who did not take the district's elementary string lessons has ever gone on to join the high school orchestra.
Not all of the students who would have taken the elementary string lessons will take private lessons instead.
Students who took the elementary lessons play better in high school than those who did not.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that losing the school lessons means losing the training that feeds the orchestra; if every would-be student simply took private lessons instead, the pipeline would be unaffected. (D) states the modest assumption that not all of them will. (A) is tempting but reverses the premise: the argument says most joiners had lessons, not that most lesson-takers joined, and it doesn't need the latter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless elementary string lessons come back, high school orchestra membership will fall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most orchestra members took the elementary lessons; the district cut those lessons last year.

breakdown.analysis: Does cutting the school lessons actually mean kids won't learn strings? What if every one of them just signs up for private lessons? Then the orchestra still gets trained players and nothing changes. We need an answer that blocks the 'they'll learn elsewhere' escape. Test by negation.

choices.note: Tempting, but it flips the premise. The argument says most joiners had lessons, not that most lesson-takers joined. Negate it: maybe only 30% of lesson-takers joined. Losing the lessons could still shrink the orchestra.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most students who took elementary string lessons went on to join the orchestra.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: cost. The argument predicts a decline; it doesn't compare the price of different fixes. Negation does nothing.
choices.negation: Restoring the lessons would not cost less than other ways of recruiting members.

choices.note: Too strong. The premise says 'most,' so some members might have skipped the lessons. Negate it and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: At least one student who did not take the district's elementary string lessons has joined the high school orchestra.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all of the students who would have taken the lessons will take private lessons instead. Then the pipeline is intact and there's no reason to expect a decline. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: All of the students who would have taken the elementary string lessons will take private lessons instead.

choices.note: Skill isn't the issue; the argument is about how many students join. Negate it and the membership argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Students who took the elementary lessons do not play better in high school than those who did not.

questions.stimulus: A certain species of oak grows an unusually thick, spongy bark. The tree is native to dry hillsides where wildfires sweep through every few decades, and a thick layer of bark insulates a tree's living tissue from the heat of a passing fire. Some botanists therefore conclude that this oak's bark is probably an adaptation that protects the tree from fire.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the botanists' argument?
choices: Most wildfires in the oak's native range burn through the undergrowth on the hillsides without ever reaching the treetops.
Oaks of this species whose bark has been stripped are more likely than others to die in wildfires.
Some trees from regions that rarely burn also have thick, insulating bark.
The spongy bark stores rainwater during the wet season and releases it to the tree through summer droughts.
Growing thick bark diverts resources a tree could otherwise use to grow taller or produce more acorns.
questions.explanation: The botanists infer a trait's function from the fact that it would help with fire. (D) offers a different job the spongy bark does, storing water for droughts, which gives another explanation for why the trait evolved. (B) is tempting but strengthens the argument by showing that bark does protect against fire. (C) is the subtler near-miss: other trees' bark doesn't tell us why this oak's bark evolved.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: This oak's thick, spongy bark is probably an adaptation for fire protection.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The oak lives where wildfires happen; thick bark insulates against heat.

breakdown.analysis: Just because a trait could help with fire, does that mean that's what it's for? Lots of traits fit more than one story. This is a function guess, and the standard way to weaken one is to give the trait a different job. It's like deciding a dog's thick coat is for protection from thorns when it's really for warmth. We need an answer that offers another explanation for spongy bark.

choices.note: This doesn't touch the bark. If anything, ground fires reaching the trunk would make thick bark more useful, so it leans toward the botanists.
Tempting, because it's about bark and fire. But it shows bark does protect against fire, so it strengthens. Wrong direction.
Tempting, because it suggests thick bark can exist without fire. But other trees' bark could have evolved for other reasons; that doesn't tell us why THIS oak's bark evolved. Wrong group.

CORRECT. Now there's a second job for the bark: the 'spongy' part stores water for droughts. That gives a strong alternative explanation for why the oak evolved this trait, so the fire story is less likely to be the reason.
So? Every trait has costs. A cost doesn't say what the benefit is for, and it fits a fire story just as well.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: One engineer has defined a robot as any machine that senses its surroundings and acts on what it senses without moment-to-moment human direction. But consider an ordinary household thermostat: it senses the temperature of a room and switches the furnace on or off with no one directing it. Yet no one would call a thermostat a robot.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that a proposed definition is too narrow because it excludes some machines that are clearly robots
proposing a more precise definition that avoids the difficulty the argument identifies
appealing to the judgment of the engineers who actually design, build, and program robots
describing a case that meets all of a proposed definition's conditions but falls outside the category being defined
showing that the conditions laid down by a definition, though necessary for something to be a robot, are not sufficient
questions.explanation: The thermostat satisfies the engineer's conditions (it senses and acts without human direction) yet isn't a robot, showing the definition is too broad; (D) describes this. (E) is the near-miss: the case does show the conditions aren't sufficient, but the philosopher never shows they are necessary. (A) reverses the direction: the definition lets in too much rather than leaving out real robots.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Implicit) The engineer's definition of 'robot' is flawed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A thermostat senses and acts without human direction, so it fits the definition; but nobody calls a thermostat a robot.

breakdown.analysis: Is the thermostat a robot that the definition leaves out, or a non-robot the definition lets in? It's a non-robot that gets in. That's a case showing the definition is too broad. A definition can fail two ways: too broad (includes things it shouldn't) or too narrow (excludes things it should). We need an answer that describes a case fitting the definition but not the category, and that claims nothing more.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the right method (a case tested against a definition) with the direction reversed. A thermostat isn't a robot being shut out; it's a non-robot being let in. That's too broad, not too narrow.
choices.example: Example of this method: The engineer says robots must have arms. But a self-driving delivery cart has no arms, and it's clearly a robot.

choices.note: No new definition appears. The philosopher only shows the old one fails.
choices.example: Example of this method: The definition includes thermostats, so let's define a robot as a machine that senses, acts, and can change its own goals.

choices.note: The appeal is to ordinary usage ('no one would call'), not to engineers or any experts.
choices.example: Example of this method: Robotics engineers don't consider thermostats robots, so the definition is wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. The thermostat meets both conditions, sensing and acting without moment-to-moment direction, yet it isn't a robot. That's a case showing the definition is too broad.

Tempting, because half of it is right: the thermostat shows the conditions aren't sufficient. But the philosopher says nothing to show they're necessary; a robot that lacked one of them is never discussed. One extra claim sinks it.
choices.example: Example of this method: Every robot senses and acts on its own, as all engineers agree, but a thermostat does too and isn't a robot, so these conditions are needed but not enough.

questions.stimulus: When the Corrigan supermarket chain cut the price of its own-brand olive oil by 25 percent last spring, it expected sales of the oil to rise substantially. Instead, sales fell over the following months, even though the prices of competing brands at Corrigan stores did not change and the oil itself was not altered in any way.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why sales of Corrigan's own-brand olive oil fell?
choices: Before the price cut, Corrigan's own-brand olive oil was already the least expensive olive oil sold in its stores.
Many shoppers who buy olive oil judge its quality largely by its price.
Olive oil sales at other supermarket chains in the region rose somewhat last spring.
Corrigan advertised the price cut prominently, both in its weekly flyers and on signs posted throughout its stores.
Corrigan's suppliers raised what they charged it for olive oil.
questions.explanation: If shoppers read a low price as a sign of low quality, a deep price cut could make the oil look inferior and drive buyers to other brands, explaining the drop (B). (A) is tempting, but already being the cheapest gives no reason why becoming even cheaper would lose sales. (D) deepens the puzzle, since advertising should have helped.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Corrigan cut its own-brand olive oil price by 25%, but sales fell, with competitors' prices and the oil itself unchanged.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a cheaper product sell less? The stimulus rules out the easy answers: competitors didn't cut prices, and the oil didn't change. So the explanation must be about how shoppers react to the price itself. Common sense helps: lots of people assume cheap means worse. We need an answer that makes a lower price a reason to buy less.

choices.note: Tempting, because it seems to matter that it was already cheapest. But it doesn't explain why getting even cheaper would cost sales. It leaves the puzzle in place.
CORRECT. If shoppers use price as a quality signal, a 25% cut makes the oil look worse, so some switch to pricier brands. That explains falling sales without contradicting anything.
This makes it stranger: oil was selling well elsewhere, so the fall at Corrigan isn't a general market slump.
This deepens the puzzle. More shoppers knew about the lower price, so sales should have risen.
Wrong dimension: Corrigan's costs. What Corrigan paid suppliers doesn't explain why shoppers bought less.

questions.stimulus: According to company records, 20 percent of the items that Pardoe Outfitters' customers ordered online last year were returned for refunds or exchanges, compared with only 5 percent of the items bought in Pardoe's stores. So Pardoe's returns staff spent more of their time last year processing returns of online orders than processing returns of in-store purchases.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that customers who return items are generally dissatisfied with the company's products or service
fails to consider that some of the company's customers shop both online and in its stores
fails to consider that many items ordered online may have been returned at one of the company's stores rather than by mail
overlooks the possibility that the stores sold far more items than were ordered online
takes for granted that returned items cannot be resold at full price
questions.explanation: A higher return rate doesn't mean more returns: if in-store sales vastly outnumber online orders, 5 percent of a large number can exceed 20 percent of a small one, and the staff's time tracks the number of returns. (D) points this out. (C) is tempting because it raises a channel complication, but the conclusion is about returns of online orders wherever they were handed in, so it changes nothing. (B) is irrelevant for a similar reason.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Returns staff spent more time on online returns than on in-store returns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 20% of online items were returned vs. 5% of in-store items.

breakdown.analysis: Does a higher percentage mean a bigger pile of returns? Not if the bases differ. Imagine 1,000 online items (200 returns) and 10,000 in-store items (500 returns). The online rate is four times higher, but the staff handled more in-store returns. Watch the switch from a rate to an absolute amount; it's a classic, know it. We need an answer that says the argument ignores how many items each channel sold. Note the key never says 'percent' or 'number'; it says the stores sold far more, which is the same point in different words.

choices.note: Customer satisfaction never comes up. The argument is about staff time.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Twice as many online items were returned, so our online customers must dislike us.

choices.note: It sounds like a complication, but it doesn't matter who made the purchases; what matters is how many returns of each type there were.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Online shoppers return more items, so the people who shop online must be pickier (ignoring that the same people also shop in the store).

choices.note: Tempting, because it borrows the stimulus's online/in-store split and hints the categories are muddled. But the conclusion is about returns of online orders versus returns of in-store purchases, however they came back. Where an online item was dropped off doesn't change how many of each kind the staff processed.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most returns were handed in at our stores, so most returned items must have been bought in our stores.

choices.note: CORRECT. Rates don't tell you totals. If the stores sold far more items, 5% of them could be more returns than 20% of the online orders, and then the staff would spend more time on in-store returns.
The argument never assumes anything about reselling. Irrelevant to staff time.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Returns cost us money, since every returned item has to be thrown away.

questions.stimulus: A delivery drone may be licensed by the regional aviation office to fly over residential neighborhoods only if it passes the office's noise test, and no drone without a sound-dampening shroud has ever passed that test. The Skylet drone, which several retailers hope to use for home deliveries next year, has four exposed propellers and no shroud of any kind. So the Skylet will not be licensed to fly over residential neighborhoods next year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The Skylet will not be fitted with a sound-dampening shroud of any kind before next year.
No drone that lacks a sound-dampening shroud could possibly pass the noise test, whatever its other features.
Any drone that is equipped with a sound-dampening shroud can pass the noise test.
Most drones with exposed propellers would fail the noise test even if they were fitted with shrouds.
If the Skylet is not licensed to fly over residential neighborhoods, retailers will not use it for home deliveries next year.
questions.explanation: The evidence is about drones without shrouds, and the Skylet has none now; the argument needs it to stay that way until next year. If it gets a shroud first, the track record of shroudless drones no longer bears on it, so (A) is required. (B) is the tempting too-strong version: it would help, but the argument rests on the fact that no shroudless drone ever has passed, not on its being impossible.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Skylet won't be licensed to fly over residential neighborhoods next year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Licensed → passes noise test; no shroudless drone has ever passed; the Skylet has no shroud.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: Licensed → Passed test. No shroudless drone has ever passed. The Skylet is shroudless today. But the conclusion is about NEXT year. What if the maker bolts on a shroud before then? Then the 'no shroudless drone has passed' evidence doesn't apply to it at all. We need an answer that keeps the Skylet in the shroudless group. Test every choice by negation.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the Skylet will be fitted with a shroud before next year. Then it's no longer a shroudless drone, the track record says nothing about it, and the conclusion loses its support.
choices.negation: The Skylet will be fitted with a sound-dampening shroud of some kind before next year.

choices.note: Tempting, because it would make the argument airtight. But the argument doesn't need 'could not possibly.' Negate it: some shroudless drone could pass in principle. The argument still stands on the record that none ever has. Too strong to be required.
choices.negation: Some drone that lacks a sound-dampening shroud could pass the noise test.

choices.note: About drones WITH shrouds, which the argument never relies on. Negate it: some shrouded drones fail. No effect on a shroudless Skylet.
choices.negation: Some drone equipped with a sound-dampening shroud cannot pass the noise test.

choices.note: Again about drones fitted with shrouds, and 'most' on top. Negate it and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most drones with exposed propellers would fail even with shrouds.

choices.note: This is about what happens after the conclusion: whether retailers use the drone. The argument stops at licensing. Negation does nothing.
choices.negation: Retailers might use the Skylet for home deliveries next year even if it is not licensed to fly over residential neighborhoods.

questions.stimulus: Cartographer: We must issue a corrected edition of our trail map of the Elk Basin area, even though the error affects only one trail and no one has complained about it. The map shows a footbridge across a creek, but the bridge washed away last spring, and hikers planning routes from our map could count on that bridge being there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the cartographer's position?
choices: Any error that could mislead a publication's users should be corrected, even a minor one that no one has reported.
A mapmaker should issue a corrected edition whenever a user complains about an error in the map.
A mapmaker need not correct an error in a published map unless the error could endanger the people who use the map.
Errors in a published map should be corrected only if many of the map's users are likely to be affected by them.
A mapmaker should verify every feature shown on a map in person before the map is first published or reissued.
questions.explanation: The cartographer says a correction is required even though the error is small and nobody has complained, because hikers could rely on it. (A) requires correcting any error that could mislead users and explicitly sets aside both the error's size and the lack of complaints. (C) is the trap: a washed-out bridge might well endanger hikers, but 'need not unless' gives only a necessary condition for the duty, so it never says the map MUST be corrected. (D) is also an 'only if' condition, and with one trail affected it points the other way.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mapmaker must issue a corrected edition.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The map shows a bridge that is gone; hikers could rely on it when planning routes. (Granted: only one trail is affected, and no one has complained.)

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to deliver the conclusion: a correction is REQUIRED. It also has to survive the two facts the cartographer concedes: the error is small, and no one has complained. Watch the logic words. 'Need not X unless Y' and 'X only if Y' give necessary conditions: they can tell you when you're off the hook, never when you're obligated. Here, an answer that would merely be consistent with correcting the map isn't enough.

choices.note: CORRECT. The missing bridge is an error that could mislead the map's users (hikers planning routes), and both concessions are neutralized ('even a minor one,' 'no one has reported'). Verdict: it should be corrected.
The condition isn't met: nobody has complained. With the trigger absent, this principle says nothing.

Tempting, because a washed-out bridge sounds dangerous, so the 'unless' clause seems satisfied. But 'need not correct unless it could endanger' only says danger is required for a duty. It never says danger creates one. The principle would be the right kind of answer for 'which is consistent with,' not for 'justify.'
Another necessary condition, and the facts point against meeting it: only one trail is affected. If anything this supports leaving the map alone.
Good advice, but it's about checking features before publication, not about what to do once an error is found. It doesn't require the correction the cartographer insists on.

questions.stimulus: Most of the antique clocks in a certain museum's collection were made before 1850, and every clock in the collection that was made before 1850 has a brass movement. Every brass-movement clock in the collection that has been restored keeps accurate time. Yet fewer than half of the clocks in the collection keep accurate time.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Most of the clocks in the collection that were made before 1850 have not been restored.
Every clock in the collection that keeps accurate time is a brass-movement clock that has been restored.
The collection includes at least one clock with a brass movement that has never been restored.
At least one clock in the collection that keeps accurate time was made after 1850.
No clock in the collection made after 1850 has a brass movement.
questions.explanation: More than half the clocks are pre-1850 and fewer than half keep accurate time, so at least one pre-1850 clock doesn't keep time; it has a brass movement, and a restored brass clock would keep time, so it is an unrestored brass clock (C). (A) is the dominant trap: the numbers guarantee one unrestored clock, not most. (B) reverses the restored-brass conditional.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most clocks in the collection were made before 1850; 2. made before 1850 → brass movement; 3. brass movement AND restored → keeps accurate time; 4. fewer than half the clocks keep accurate time.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so do the counting. Say there are 100 clocks. More than 50 were made before 1850, but fewer than 50 keep accurate time. So at least one pre-1850 clock does NOT keep accurate time. That clock has a brass movement (fact 2). Contrapositive of fact 3: not accurate → NOT (brass AND restored). It is brass, so it hasn't been restored. That's all the numbers guarantee: ONE such clock, not most. Most students pick (A), because 'most were made before 1850' plus 'fewer than half keep time' feels like it should give 'most pre-1850 clocks are unrestored.' It doesn't: 60 pre-1850 clocks with 45 of them restored (and accurate) fits every fact, and then most pre-1850 clocks ARE restored. 'Some' is not 'most.' The right answer also hides: it never mentions 1850, so it looks off topic until you trace the chain.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the right idea at the wrong strength. Try 100 clocks: 60 made before 1850, 45 of those restored and accurate, 15 not. Fewer than half keep time, yet most pre-1850 clocks are restored. The facts force one unrestored clock, not most.
This reverses fact 3. Restored brass clocks keep accurate time, but nothing says they're the only clocks that do. A clock with some other movement could keep accurate time too.

CORRECT. Some pre-1850 clock must fail to keep accurate time, since more than half the clocks are pre-1850 and fewer than half keep time. That clock has a brass movement, and a restored brass clock would keep time, so it has never been restored.
We don't know this. Every accurate clock could have been made before 1850; nothing requires a later clock to keep time.
We don't know this. The facts say every pre-1850 clock is brass; they say nothing about later clocks, which could have brass movements too.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the lichens that once covered the old stone walls of a village churchyard have almost entirely disappeared. Botanists attribute the loss to exhaust from the bypass road that opened beside the churchyard eleven years ago. Lichens have no roots and draw water and nutrients directly from the air, so they take in whatever pollutants the air carries.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the botanists' argument EXCEPT:
choices: Lichens on the gravestones in the same churchyard, which are screened from the road by a dense yew hedge, have largely survived.
The walls nearest the bypass lost their lichens first, and those farthest from it lost theirs last.
Because lichens grow extremely slowly, a wall that has lost its lichens may take decades to be fully recolonized.
The lichen species on the walls are known to be unusually sensitive to compounds found in vehicle exhaust.
Records kept by a local naturalists' society show that the lichen cover on the walls had changed little in the forty years before the bypass opened.
questions.explanation: Four choices make exhaust a likelier cause: a screened comparison group that survived (A), a gradient running away from the road (B), a known sensitivity (D), and a stable baseline that ended when the road opened (E). (C) explains why the walls haven't recovered, which says nothing about what killed the lichens in the first place, so it is the exception. Many students cross off (A) or (E) because neither mentions exhaust directly.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Exhaust from the bypass caused the churchyard's lichens to disappear.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The lichens vanished over the decade since the road opened; lichens absorb whatever pollutants are in the air.

breakdown.analysis: In an EXCEPT question, four answers strengthen and one doesn't. So hunt for the dud. Ways to strengthen a cause: show the effect is missing where the cause is blocked, show the effect tracks the cause's intensity, give a mechanism, or show nothing changed until the cause arrived. Here the strengtheners are dressed up (a hedge, a naturalists' log), so don't eliminate them just because they don't say 'exhaust.' The dud is the one about what happens AFTER the lichens are gone.

choices.note: Strengthens. The gravestones are in the same churchyard but shielded from the road, and their lichens survived. That's a built-in comparison: same place, same weather, less exhaust, no loss.
Strengthens. Damage that spreads outward from the road is what you'd expect if the road is the source.

CORRECT. This is the exception. Slow regrowth explains why the walls are still bare, but it says nothing about what caused the loss. It would be just as true if the lichens had been killed by drought or by cleaning.
Strengthens. It supplies the mechanism: these particular lichens are especially vulnerable to what cars emit.
Strengthens, though it's easy to miss. Forty stable years followed by a collapse right after the road opened ties the timing of the loss to the road and makes a long-running natural decline unlikely.

questions.stimulus: Each year a consumer magazine prices the same basket of forty common grocery items at the twelve largest supermarkets in the county. This year, as in each of the three previous years, the basket cost less at Brockway Foods than at any of the other eleven stores. So whatever grocery item a county shopper buys, it costs less at Brockway than at any of those other eleven stores.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that shoppers in the county decide where to buy groceries solely on the basis of the prices that stores charge
takes for granted that the magazine priced the basket at the same time of year in each of the four years
draws a conclusion about every supermarket in the county from data about only the twelve largest of them
overlooks the possibility that a store whose basket costs least overall charges more than its rivals for some items
infers that Brockway will keep the lowest prices in future years from its having had them four years running
questions.explanation: The data compare the TOTAL cost of a basket; the conclusion is about EVERY single item. A store can win on the total while charging more than a rival for some of the items, which is the possibility (D) says the argument overlooks. (C) is the main trap: the conclusion is limited to the other eleven stores, so no claim is made about smaller supermarkets. (E) attacks a prediction the argument never makes, and (A) and (B) raise assumptions the conclusion doesn't depend on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Any grocery item costs less at Brockway than at the other eleven large supermarkets.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The magazine's forty-item basket cost less in total at Brockway than at any of the other eleven, this year and the three before.

breakdown.analysis: Does the cheapest basket mean the cheapest everything? No. A total can be lowest even if some of its parts are higher. Imagine Brockway charges a dollar less for coffee but a dime more for milk: its basket wins, and milk is still dearer there. This is a whole-to-part flaw (sometimes called division): what's true of a total isn't automatically true of each piece. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says a store with the cheapest basket could still charge more for some items. The four-year streak is filler: it makes the data feel solid, but solid data about totals still say nothing about each item.

choices.note: So? The conclusion is about what items cost at each store, not about why shoppers pick a store. Nothing in the argument assumes price is a shopper's only reason.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Brockway is the cheapest store, so every shopper in the county must shop there.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Even if the timing varied from year to year, this year's result alone supports 'Brockway's basket is cheapest.' The gap is between the basket's total and each item, which timing doesn't touch.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Prices were checked in December one year and in June the next, yet the two surveys are compared as though nothing else changed.

choices.note: Tempting, because the magazine checked only the twelve largest stores. But read the conclusion: it compares Brockway only with 'those other eleven stores.' It makes no claim about smaller supermarkets.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Brockway beat the eleven other large stores, so no grocer in the county, not even a corner shop, is cheaper.

choices.note: CORRECT. The basket's total is cheapest at Brockway, but that's consistent with Brockway charging more for some items in it. The argument moves from a fact about a whole to a claim about each of its parts.
The conclusion is about what things cost now ('it costs less'), not about future years. The four-year record is background, not the basis for a prediction.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Brockway has been cheapest four years running, so it will surely be cheapest next year.

questions.stimulus: Biographer: Letters I found while researching my life of a late composer reveal that her younger brother, who has since died, served two years in prison for fraud. I will leave this out of the book. His crime had nothing to do with her music or her career, and making it public would deeply hurt his children, who are still living and who had no part in the fraud.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the biographer's decision?
choices: A biographer should omit a fact about a subject's relative if the fact has no bearing on the subject's work and would distress that relative.
A biographer should include every accurate fact found in a subject's private papers unless including it would distress someone still living.
Facts that shed light on a subject's work belong in a biography even when they cause distress.
Biographers should not draw on private letters unless the families of those who wrote them consent.
A biographer should withhold a discreditable truth unrelated to the subject's achievements if revealing it would hurt people who bear no blame for it.
questions.explanation: (E) matches every fact in abstract terms: a discreditable truth (the brother's fraud), unrelated to the subject's achievements (nothing to do with her music or career), whose disclosure would hurt blameless people (his children), and it prescribes withholding it. (A) is the dominant trap: it fits the irrelevance, but its distress condition is about the relative the fact concerns, and the brother has died; the people who would be hurt are his children. (B) uses 'unless,' so it says nothing about what to do when someone would be distressed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The biographer will leave the brother's imprisonment out of the book.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. The crime had nothing to do with the composer's music or career; 2. publishing it would hurt the brother's living children, who had no part in it.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says (leave it out), and its conditions have to match the facts exactly. List the facts: the brother is dead; the crime is irrelevant to her work; the people who'd be hurt are his children, who are alive and blameless. Now check each condition word by word. Most students pick (A), because it covers both of the biographer's reasons in nearly the stimulus's own words. But read who must be distressed: 'that relative,' meaning the brother. He has died, so the condition isn't met and (A) never applies. The right answer is harder to like because it talks about a 'discreditable truth' and 'people who bear no blame' instead of brothers and children.

choices.note: Tempting, and the most popular wrong answer. It covers irrelevance, and it covers distress, but the distress must be to 'that relative,' the brother the fact is about. He has died. The people who'd be hurt are his children. One swapped party and the principle doesn't apply.

Tempting, because it mentions distress to someone living. But 'include unless distress' only tells you what to do when there's NO distress (include). When there is distress, it's silent. It never tells the biographer to leave anything out.
Wrong case. This is about facts that shed light on the work, and the biographer says this fact doesn't. It doesn't apply here, and if it did, it would point toward including.
Wrong dimension. The decision is about mentioning a fact, not about using letters as sources. The biographer has already used the letters, and consent never comes up.

CORRECT. Discreditable truth: a prison term for fraud. Unrelated to the subject's achievements: nothing to do with her music or career. Hurts people who bear no blame: the children, who had no part in the fraud. Verdict: withhold. Every condition is met, and the verdict is the biographer's decision.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Three years ago the city rezoned the Millbrook Road corridor to forbid any new building taller than four stories. In the decade before the rezoning, five office buildings went up along the corridor, every one of them taller than four stories; in the three years since, not one office building of any height has gone up there. Evidently, the rezoning has discouraged office development along the corridor.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the council member's argument depends?
choices: Most developers who build office buildings in the city would prefer, other things being equal, to build ones taller than four stories.
Demand for office space in the city as a whole has not declined at all over the past three years.
When the rezoning took effect, the corridor still had land on which an office building could have been put up.
The rezoning was adopted chiefly in order to discourage further office development along the corridor.
No new residential buildings of any height have gone up along the corridor since the rezoning either.
questions.explanation: The argument credits the height limit with the halt in office construction, so it must assume the halt wasn't forced by something else, such as the corridor simply having no room left after five new buildings. (C) states that minimal precondition: there was still somewhere to build. (B) is the tempting too-strong defender: a slight dip in demand wouldn't hurt the argument, so 'not declined at all' isn't required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rezoning discouraged office development along the corridor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Before the four-story limit, five tall office buildings went up in a decade; since the limit, no office building of any height in three years.

breakdown.analysis: Before/after with a policy in the middle, so the argument assumes the policy, not something else, made the difference. Prephrase the usual suspects: demand fell, or there was nothing left to build on. The second is easy to miss: five buildings in a decade might have used up the corridor's available lots. If no site was left, nothing would be built with or without the height limit. Negation is the test: the right answer, negated, should wreck the argument; a too-strong answer, negated, barely scratches it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it explains how a height limit could deter builders. But it's not required: negate it and only some developers prefer tall buildings, which is enough for the limit to deter some of them. The argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most developers would prefer to build office buildings taller than four stories.

choices.note: Tempting: falling demand is the obvious alternative cause, so a defender against it looks required. But 'not declined at all' is too strong. Negate it: demand dipped slightly. A slight dip doesn't explain a total halt, so the argument still stands.
choices.negation: Demand for office space in the city as a whole has declined at least somewhat over the past three years.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: when the limit took effect, there was no land left on the corridor for an office building. Then nothing would have been built no matter what the zoning said, and the rezoning can't be what discouraged development. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: When the rezoning took effect, the corridor had no land left on which an office building could have been put up.

choices.note: Why the council adopted the rule doesn't matter; what matters is its effect. Negate it and the argument is unchanged.
choices.negation: The rezoning was not adopted chiefly to discourage office development along the corridor.

choices.note: Not required, and if true it would hint at a general slowdown, which hurts the argument. Negate it (some housing went up) and the argument is fine, or even helped.
choices.negation: At least one new residential building has gone up along the corridor since the rezoning.

questions.stimulus: A survey of a representative sample of the people who visited the Ondine Hill nature reserve last year found that only 8 percent of them had brought a dog on any of their visits. The reserve's managers concluded that banning dogs from the trails would only slightly reduce the number of visits the reserve receives, even if everyone who brings a dog stopped coming.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the managers' argument?
choices: Many of the people who bring dogs to the reserve say they would keep visiting it without their dogs if dogs were banned.
People who brought dogs to the reserve last year came, on average, far more often than did the other visitors.
Some people who now avoid the reserve because of dogs on the trails would start visiting it if dogs were banned.
At other nature reserves in the region, the share of visitors who bring dogs is considerably higher than 8 percent.
Of all the problems the reserve's managers deal with, damage caused by dogs is the most costly to repair.
questions.explanation: The survey counts people; the conclusion is about visits. If the 8 percent who bring dogs come far more often than everyone else, they could account for a large share of all visits, and losing them would cut visits substantially (B). (A) and (C) are the traps: they mention dog owners and the ban, but each makes the drop in visits even smaller, so they strengthen. The sample is stipulated to be representative, so there is no sampling flaw to exploit.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Even if every dog-bringer stopped coming, the number of visits would fall only slightly.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only 8% of last year's visitors (people, from a representative sample) brought a dog.

breakdown.analysis: Most students hunt for a biased sample, but the stimulus says the sample was representative. Look at the units instead. The premise is about PEOPLE: 8% of visitors. The conclusion is about VISITS. Those are different counts. Picture 92 people who each come once a year and 8 people who walk their dogs there every day: the dog walkers make nearly 3,000 visits to the others' 92. We need an answer that makes the 8% of people a much bigger share of visits. The right answer never says 'visits' and 'people' are different; you have to see why frequency matters.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about dog owners and the ban. But if they keep coming without their dogs, the drop in visits is even smaller. That helps the managers.
CORRECT. If dog owners visit far more often, 8% of the people could make up a large share of the visits. Then losing all of them could cut visits sharply, and 'only slightly' fails.
Tempting, because it says the ban could change who visits. But it adds visits, making the managers' prediction look even safer. Wrong direction.
Irrelevant comparison. Other reserves' numbers don't change what share of THIS reserve's visits come from dog owners.
True or not, it's about the cost of dog damage, a reason someone might want a ban. It says nothing about how many visits the reserve would lose.

questions.stimulus: Lexicographer: Some have proposed that the national dictionary admit a new word only after it has appeared in at least three major newspapers. Admittedly, such a rule would screen out many passing fads. But many regional farming and fishing terms, though spoken for generations, almost never reach print. A dictionary's chief purpose is to record the language as it is actually used, so the proposal should be rejected, since the rule would exclude a good many words in active use.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the lexicographer's argument by the claim that the rule would exclude a good many words in active use?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, which is supported by the claim that a dictionary's chief purpose is to record actual usage.
It is a conclusion that the argument supports by citing a class of cases and then uses, along with a general claim about dictionaries, to support its main conclusion.
It is a premise for which the argument offers no support and which, together with a claim about a dictionary's purpose, supports the main conclusion.
It is a consideration that the argument concedes counts in the proposal's favor but holds is outweighed.
It is a subsidiary conclusion offered in support of the claim that a dictionary's chief purpose is to record the language as it is actually used.
questions.explanation: The claim arrives after 'since,' so it looks like a bare premise, but the farming-and-fishing sentence is evidence for it: those terms are words in active use that rarely reach print. So it is supported, and it then joins the claim about a dictionary's purpose to support rejecting the proposal (B). (C) is the dominant trap: it gets the claim's job right but says it receives no support. (D) describes the concession about passing fads.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The proposal should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Many regional terms in long use rarely reach print; 2. so the rule would exclude many words in active use; 3. a dictionary's chief purpose is to record actual usage. (Concession: the rule would screen out fads.)

breakdown.analysis: Find the main conclusion first: 'the proposal should be rejected.' Then ask, for the claim in question, two things: does anything support it, and what does it support? The indicator 'since' tells you it supports the conclusion. Don't stop there. Why would the rule exclude many words in active use? Because regional terms spoken for generations almost never reach print. That sentence is evidence for our claim. So the claim is both supported and supporting: a subsidiary conclusion. Most students pick (C), because 'since' screams 'premise' and the claim sits at the very end. It fails on one phrase: 'offers no support.' The right answer is hard to like because it calls the farming terms 'a class of cases,' which you have to translate.

choices.note: Wrong conclusion. The main conclusion is that the proposal should be rejected; this claim is one of the reasons for that.

CORRECT. Supported by a class of cases (regional terms that never reach print), and then used, with the general claim about what dictionaries are for, to support rejecting the proposal. Right role, right relations.

Tempting, and the most popular wrong answer. It gets the claim's job right: it does team up with the purpose claim to support the conclusion. But 'offers no support' is false. The farming-and-fishing sentence is exactly the support. One phrase sinks it.
This describes a different sentence: 'such a rule would screen out many passing fads' is the concession. Our claim counts against the proposal, not for it.
Right role, wrong relation. It is a subsidiary conclusion, but it supports rejecting the proposal, not the claim about a dictionary's purpose, which is offered on its own.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Opponents of the proposed tariff on imported steel argue that it would hurt the region's manufacturers. Admittedly, manufacturers who buy imported steel would pay more for it. But most of the region's manufacturers buy no imported steel at all; they use only steel produced in this country. So the tariff is unlikely to raise costs for most of the region's manufacturers.
questions.stem: The economist's argument is flawed because it
choices: takes for granted that manufacturers who now buy imported steel could not avoid the tariff by switching to domestic steel
infers that the tariff would hurt none of the region's manufacturers from the fact that most of them buy no imported steel
presumes, without providing justification, that domestic steel mills could supply all the steel the region's manufacturers need
overlooks the possibility that making one source of a good more expensive could allow other sources to charge more for it
treats the opponents' failure to prove that the tariff would be harmful as evidence that it would not be
questions.explanation: The economist reasons that because most manufacturers buy only domestic steel, the tariff won't touch their costs. But a tariff that makes imported steel dearer can let domestic producers raise their prices too, which would raise costs for exactly those manufacturers. (D) describes this in general terms. (A) is something the argument doesn't need: if importers could switch, that would only help the economist. (C) sounds like D's supply story, but the argument never relies on domestic mills' capacity; the domestic-only buyers already get their steel. (B) overstates a conclusion limited to 'most' and 'unlikely,' and (E) names a flaw the economist doesn't commit.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tariff probably won't raise costs for most of the region's manufacturers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most of them buy only domestic steel. (Concession: buyers of imported steel would pay more.)

breakdown.analysis: Ask what the tariff could do to manufacturers who never touch imported steel. Their costs depend on what domestic steelmakers charge. And once foreign steel gets pricier, what stops domestic steelmakers from raising their prices? Nothing in the argument. It's like saying a toll on one bridge won't affect people who use the other bridge, when the other bridge's traffic, and its own toll, may go up. The right answer is hard to like because it never mentions steel, tariffs, or the region; it's a structural description you have to map back onto the argument.

choices.note: Tempting, because switching sounds like the kind of market response the argument ignores. But the argument doesn't rely on importers being stuck. It concedes they'd pay more for imported steel, and if they could switch, that would only make the economist's case stronger. A presumption that helps the other side isn't the flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The bridge toll will cost commuters money, since none of them could possibly take the free road instead.

choices.note: Tempting, because the step from 'most buy no imported steel' to a conclusion about manufacturers looks shaky. But the economist concludes only that costs are UNLIKELY to rise for MOST of them, not that none will be hurt. This attacks a stronger conclusion than the one drawn.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most of the town's shops close on Sundays, so no shop will be affected by the Sunday parking ban.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about domestic supply, which is where the real problem lives. But the argument never depends on how much domestic mills can produce: the manufacturers it calls safe already buy all their steel at home. The flaw is about domestic PRICES, not capacity, and mills with plenty of capacity could still raise prices.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Everyone can just buy local tomatoes instead, as though the local farms could grow enough for the whole city.

choices.note: CORRECT. Imported steel is one source, domestic steel another. Make the first more expensive and domestic producers may be free to charge more as well, raising costs for the very manufacturers the economist calls safe.
A familiar flaw, but not this one. The economist doesn't rest on the opponents' lack of proof; the economist offers positive evidence about where manufacturers buy steel.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: No one has proved the tariff will hurt anyone, so it won't.

questions.stimulus: At the Oakmere Foundation, every applicant for a research grant who submits a detailed budget is interviewed, and no applicant receives a grant without first being interviewed. This year, most of the applicants who received grants had not submitted detailed budgets, and most of the applicants who submitted detailed budgets did not receive grants.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most of the applicants whom the foundation interviewed this year were not awarded grants.
Some applicants who submitted detailed budgets this year were not interviewed by the foundation.
Submitting a detailed budget made an applicant less likely to receive a grant from the foundation this year.
Most of the applicants who were interviewed this year had not submitted detailed budgets.
Not everyone the foundation interviewed this year had submitted a detailed budget.
questions.explanation: Everyone who received a grant was interviewed, and most grant recipients had no detailed budget, so at least one person was interviewed without having submitted a budget: not everyone interviewed had submitted one (E). (D) is the too-strong version: those budgetless recipients could be a small fraction of all interviewees, since every budget submitter was interviewed too. (A) fails for a similar reason, and (C) reads a cause into a pattern of numbers.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Submitted budget → interviewed; 2. received grant → interviewed; 3. most grant recipients had no budget; 4. most budget submitters got no grant.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so combine the facts in pairs. Facts 2 and 3: most recipients had no budget, and every recipient was interviewed, so SOME interviewees had no budget. Facts 1 and 4: most budget submitters got nothing, and all of them were interviewed, so SOME interviewees got no grant. Those 'some' statements are all you can be sure of. The traps upgrade 'some' to 'most.' Test with numbers: 100 budget submitters (10 funded) and 21 recipients (11 without budgets). Interviewees: at least 111, only 11 of them budgetless. So (D) fails. Now try 10 submitters (2 funded) and 30 recipients (28 without budgets): about 38 interviewees, 30 funded. So (A) fails. The right answer is a double negative; translate it: at least one interviewee had no budget.

choices.note: Tempting, because most budget submitters were turned down. But the interviewees also include every grant recipient. With 10 submitters (8 turned down) and 30 recipients, most interviewees got grants. Not forced.
This contradicts fact 1: every applicant who submits a detailed budget is interviewed.
An unwarranted causal claim. The numbers describe who got grants; they don't show the budget lowered anyone's chances. Applicants who submit budgets may differ in other ways.

Tempting: it's the right idea at the wrong strength. Some interviewees had no budget, but all budget submitters were interviewed too, and there could be many more of them. With 100 submitters and only 11 budgetless recipients, most interviewees DID submit budgets.

CORRECT. Most grant recipients had no budget, and all recipients were interviewed, so at least one interviewee had no budget. 'Not everyone interviewed had submitted one' says exactly that, and nothing more.

questions.stimulus: Every tree that was removed from the Wexley greenbelt this year had been inspected beforehand by the county arborist, who checks trees for disease and storm damage. The old elm by the footbridge, which many residents had feared would be cut down, was not removed this year, so the arborist must not have inspected it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Every player who scored a goal for the Hawks this season attended every one of the team's practices. Dev did not attend every practice, so he did not score a goal for the Hawks this season.
Every dish on the café's menu that contains nuts is marked with a small star. The lentil soup on today's menu is marked with a star, so it must contain nuts.
Only paintings that the auction house's experts had appraised were sold at last week's auction. The river landscape went unsold, so it was never appraised.
Most of the apartments at Larkin Court that were repainted this year had been inspected by the building manager first. Unit 4 was not repainted this year, so the manager did not inspect it.
Every building demolished on Grant Avenue last year had first been condemned by the city. The city has condemned no buildings on the avenue this year, so none will be demolished there this year.
questions.explanation: The original reasons: removed → inspected; the elm wasn't removed; so it wasn't inspected. That's denying the antecedent. (C) does the same, with 'only' standing in for 'every': sold → appraised; not sold; so not appraised. (D) is the near-miss: same move, but its premise says 'most,' a weaker link than the original's 'every.' (A) is a valid contrapositive, (B) affirms the consequent, and (E) projects last year's pattern onto this year.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The arborist didn't inspect the elm.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every removed tree was inspected; the elm wasn't removed.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All X were Y; this one is not X; so it is not Y.

breakdown.analysis: Diagram it: Removed → Inspected. The elm is NOT removed, and the argument concludes NOT inspected. That's negating the sufficient condition and concluding the negation of the necessary one: denying the antecedent. Lots of trees can be inspected and left standing. Now match the skeleton exactly: same conditional, same 'every/only' strength, same move. Watch for 'only': 'Only appraised paintings were sold' means Sold → Appraised, the same direction as the original. Each wrong answer changes one thing: validity, direction, quantifier, or time frame.

choices.note: Valid. Scored → attended every practice; Dev didn't attend every practice; so he didn't score. That's the contrapositive, which is good reasoning. The original is flawed, so this can't match.
A different flaw. Nuts → star; the soup has a star; so nuts. That's affirming the consequent (reversing), not denying the antecedent.

CORRECT. Sold → appraised. The landscape was not sold, so it wasn't appraised. Same move as the elm: deny the 'sold' part and conclude the 'appraised' part is false too. The 'only' wording disguises it.

Tempting: same structure and same mistake, so it's the closest wrong answer. But the premise is 'most,' not 'every.' The original's conditional holds for all removed trees; this one's link doesn't hold even for all repainted apartments. One quantifier off.

Not the same move. This uses last year's pattern to predict this year. Even granting that condemnation always comes first, the argument's problem is projecting a past rule forward, not denying the antecedent of a stated conditional.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Some claim that a forgery skilled enough to fool every expert has as much artistic value as the original, since the two look identical. But a work's artistic value depends partly on its originality: the painter of the original solved problems no one had solved before, whereas the forger merely copied that solution. So the forgery has less artistic value than the original, and those who paid high prices for undetected forgeries paid more than the forgeries were worth.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that a forger may have to solve difficult technical problems of his or her own
rejects the opponents' premise that the two works look identical instead of challenging the inference the opponents draw from it
treats a judgment about two works' relative artistic merit as settling what one of them was worth to buyers
presumes, without providing justification, that buyers of undetected forgeries believed they were buying the original works
takes for granted that originality is the only thing that determines a work's artistic value
questions.explanation: The first conclusion (the forgery has less artistic value than the original) is reasonably supported. The second is not: from a comparison of artistic merit, the critic jumps to a claim about what buyers' purchases were worth. A forgery can be less valuable artistically than its original and still be worth what someone paid for it; (C) names this shift. (A) attacks the premise about copying. (B) misdescribes the critic, who grants that the works look identical and attacks the inference. (D) is about buyers, like the key, but what buyers believed has no bearing on what the forgeries were worth, and 'undetected' already implies it. (E) misreads 'partly' as 'only.'

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: 1. The forgery has less artistic value than the original; 2. so buyers of undetected forgeries paid more than they were worth.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Artistic value depends partly on originality; the original's painter solved new problems, while the forger copied.

breakdown.analysis: The argument has two steps, and only the second is broken. Step 1: originality counts toward artistic value, the forger copied, so the forgery has LESS artistic value. Fine. Step 2: so buyers paid MORE than the forgeries were worth. Two jumps hide here. 'Less than the original' is relative; it says nothing about how much the forgery is worth in absolute terms.
