And 'artistic value' isn't the same as what a work is worth to a buyer, which can depend on many things. Most students go after step 1, because that's where the debate is. The traps are built to catch careless reading of 'partly' and of what the critic actually grants.

choices.note: Tempting, because it challenges the claim that the forger 'merely copied.' But that's an objection to a premise, and even if forgers solve some problems, the original's painter solved the new ones. It doesn't touch the leap to price.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The copy has less value because copying takes no skill (ignoring that copying takes great skill).

choices.note: This misdescribes the argument. The critic never denies that the two works look identical. The critic accepts that and attacks the step from 'look identical' to 'equal value' by adding a factor looks can't capture, originality. That's challenging the inference, the very thing this choice says the critic fails to do.
choices.example: Example of this method: Some say the twins should be paid equally because they do the same work. But they don't do the same work: one works twice the hours.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Less artistic value than the original' is a comparison of artistic merit. 'Paid more than the forgeries were worth' is a claim about what a purchase was worth. The argument treats the first as if it settled the second.

Tempting, because it's about the buyers, the same part of the argument as the right answer. But the argument doesn't need this: what buyers believed doesn't change what the forgeries were worth, and 'undetected' already tells you the buyers didn't know. The real gap is between artistic value and worth, not the buyers' beliefs.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The buyers overpaid, because they must have thought they were getting a famous original (with nothing to show what they thought).

choices.note: A misreading of 'partly.' The critic says originality is one factor in artistic value, not the only one.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Artistic value is just originality, so a technically perfect copy has none.

questions.stimulus: All of the land deeds in the Penrith collection came to it from the county registry. Every document in the collection that was written before 1800 is on rag paper, and no document on rag paper has yellowed noticeably. So none of the collection's land deeds has yellowed noticeably.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every document in the collection that is on rag paper was written before 1800.
Most of the documents that the collection received from the county registry were written before 1800.
Any document in the collection that has yellowed noticeably was written in or after 1800.
No document that the collection received from a source other than the county registry was written before 1800.
No document in the collection written in or after 1800 came from the county registry.
questions.explanation: Chain: land deed → county registry; before 1800 → rag paper → not yellowed. The conclusion needs land deed → not yellowed, so the gap is registry → before 1800. (E) supplies it in contrapositive form (written 1800 or later → not from the registry). (D) is the near-miss: it reverses that link (before 1800 → registry). (C) already follows from the premises and adds nothing, (A) reverses a stated premise, and (B) is too weak.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Land deed → not yellowed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Land deed → from the county registry; written before 1800 → rag paper; rag paper → not yellowed.

breakdown.analysis: Line up the chain: land deed → registry ... ? ... before 1800 → rag paper → not yellowed. There's a hole in the middle: nothing connects coming from the registry to being written before 1800. We need registry → before 1800, or its contrapositive: written in or after 1800 → not from the registry. The right answer uses the contrapositive, so it reads backwards; translate before you judge. Watch for the reversal (before 1800 → registry), which uses the right two terms in the wrong direction.

choices.note: This reverses a premise. We're told pre-1800 → rag paper; this says rag paper → pre-1800. Either way, it never mentions the registry or land deeds, so it can't close the gap.
Too weak. 'Most' leaves room for a registry deed written after 1800, which might not be on rag paper and might have yellowed.

Tempting, because it echoes the conclusion's subject. But it already follows from the premises (yellowed → not rag paper → not before 1800), so assuming it adds nothing. And it says nothing about the registry.

Tempting: it links the registry and the date, the two terms we need. But it runs the wrong way. Contrapositive: before 1800 → from the registry. We need from the registry → before 1800. A registry deed from 1850 is still possible.
CORRECT. Contrapositive: from the registry → written before 1800. Now the chain runs: land deed → registry → before 1800 → rag paper → not yellowed.

questions.stimulus: Arden Farm's records show that birds eat most of the strawberries the farm loses each year, while mold spoils only a small share. So although spraying the fields with fungicide each spring would save some fruit, it will not substantially reduce the farm's annual strawberry losses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Most of the delays on the Lyle rail line are caused by signal failures rather than by track repairs. So the rail authority, despite the cost, should spend more on fixing signals than on repairing track.
Most of the traffic accidents in the town of Brisco occur on weekends. So adding police patrols on weekends would substantially reduce the total number of traffic accidents in Brisco.
Only a small share of the heat a house loses escapes through its doors; most escapes through the roof. So replacing the doors will do nothing at all to lower the house's heating bills.

Street noise accounts for nearly all of the complaints a certain hotel receives, while its breakfast accounts for very few. So although hiring a new chef would eliminate some complaints, it will not substantially reduce the number of complaints the hotel receives.

Most of the money a library spends on repairs goes to its roof, and only a little goes to its windows. So although replacing the windows would trim the repair budget somewhat, it would not substantially reduce the number of repair jobs the library needs each year.
questions.explanation: The original: most of a loss comes from one source and only a small share from another, so a fix aimed at the minor source, though it would save some, won't substantially reduce the loss. (D) matches point for point: nearly all complaints come from noise, few from breakfast, so a new chef would eliminate some complaints but won't substantially reduce the number of complaints. (E) is the strongest trap: its shares and its concession are about money, but its conclusion is about the number of repair jobs. (C) overstates ('nothing at all').

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fungicide will help a little but won't substantially reduce strawberry losses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most losses come from birds; only a small share from mold.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most of a quantity comes from source X, only a little from source Y; so a fix aimed at Y, though it helps somewhat, won't substantially reduce that same quantity.

breakdown.analysis: Strip the topic. A problem has a big source and a small source; a fix aimed only at the small source helps a little but can't make a big dent. Three things must match: the share split, the fix aimed at the SMALL source with a concession that it helps a little, and a modest prediction about the SAME quantity the shares describe. That last point is where the hardest trap lives: check that the premise, the concession and the conclusion all count the same thing.

choices.note: A different conclusion: a spending recommendation comparing two options, not a prediction that a fix aimed at the minor source won't help much.
Fix aimed at the BIG source, with the opposite prediction. And 'most accidents happen on weekends' doesn't even say patrols would prevent them.
Tempting, because the shares match and the fix targets the small source. But 'do nothing at all' overshoots: a small share is still something. The original concedes the fix would help a little.

CORRECT. Big source (street noise), small source (breakfast), fix aimed at the small one (a new chef), a concession that the fix reduces the same quantity a little ('eliminate some complaints,' like 'save some fruit'), and a prediction that it won't reduce that quantity substantially. Same skeleton in new words.

Tempting, and the closest wrong answer: it has the shares, the fix aimed at the minor source, and a concession. But the shares and the concession are about MONEY spent on repairs, while the conclusion jumps to the NUMBER of repair jobs. Window repairs could be cheap but frequent, so the windows might account for most of the jobs. In the original, the shares, the concession and the conclusion all measure the same thing.

passages.title: Poets’ recordings and the sound of the poem
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When Alfred Tennyson recited “The Charge of the Light Brigade” into an Edison phonograph in 1890, he became one of the first poets whose voice would outlast him. Archives now hold many thousands of such recordings, and a growing number of scholars treat them as the surest guide to how the poems should sound. Print, these scholars point out, fixes a poem’s words but leaves much of their timing open: a reader confronting an irregular line must decide where the stresses fall, how long to pause at a line break, and whether a dash marks a hesitation or a rush. On such matters, they contend, the poet’s own voice is the closest thing we have to a score. A favorite case is William Carlos Williams, who claimed that the three-step lines of his late poems were governed by a “variable foot,” a notion many critics have dismissed as incoherent, since a foot is by definition a fixed unit. The critic Lena Haverford answers that in Williams’s recorded readings each step of the line occupies roughly the same span of time, however many syllables it holds. The measure, on this view, was there all along; the page simply failed to show it.

This argument asks more of the recordings than they can give. A poet reading aloud is a performer, and performances answer to circumstance. Allen Ginsberg read “Howl” to audiences for some four decades, and the surviving recordings differ considerably in pace and emphasis from one occasion to the next. Which of these is the poem’s true rhythm? To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover. Nor is a poet necessarily a skilled reader. Some poets have admitted to reading in a flat, hurried manner they dislike hearing, and unease before a microphone can alter a reading in ways that owe nothing to the verse.

Moreover, a published poem addresses readers who will never hear the poet’s voice, and the page has resources of its own—line breaks, indentation, spacing, punctuation—that the poet chose deliberately. Williams, after all, set out his stepped lines on the page with evident care. When a recording seems to override such choices, it is at least as plausible that the poet was improvising as that the page was deficient. Williams’s readings tell us how he chose to perform his late poems before a microphone; whether they reveal a measure the poems possessed from the start is a separate question. Recordings are best understood, then, as documents of how a poem was heard by someone who knew it intimately: evidence that can alert us to possibilities a silent reader might miss, and that deserves the weight owed to any single performance, however privileged, of a work that exists apart from it.

passages.title: Insurance and the end of volunteer fire companies
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
For much of the nineteenth century, American cities relied for protection against fire on volunteer companies: fraternal associations, many of them drawn from the trades, that kept a hand-pumped engine, drilled together, and answered the alarm without pay. Beginning with Cincinnati in 1853, city after city disbanded these companies in favor of salaried municipal departments. The standard explanation joins two developments. The steam fire engine, introduced in the 1850s, could be worked by a few trained men rather than the dozens a hand pump required, and the volunteers had grown notorious for rivalries between companies that sometimes ended in brawls at the scene of a fire.

The historian Anika Brandt finds this explanation incomplete. Many volunteer companies, she notes, bought steam engines themselves, and complaints of rowdiness date from decades before the changeover, when they prompted no reform; nor does she find evidence that fire losses were greater under volunteer protection. What changed, Brandt argues, was the market for fire insurance. On her reading, insurers that were beginning to write policies in many cities at once came to treat a paid department as grounds for lower premiums, so that merchants and property owners—the very people who led many volunteer companies—acquired a direct financial interest in abolishing them. The interpretation is contestable, since systematic rating of cities’ fire protection was still in its infancy when the first changeovers occurred. If it holds, however, it has the merit of explaining the timing of the change, which the standard view leaves obscure: in the cities Brandt studied, she reports, the decisive council vote came soon after local underwriters signaled that they would favor a paid department. It would also explain why, as the council minutes she examined show, prominent volunteers frequently supported the measures that ended their own companies.

Yet the account leaves an important question unanswered: why did the insurers prefer paid departments? Brandt treats the insurers’ rate schedules as though they simply recorded a judgment about which kind of department fought fires better—but she has herself argued that there is little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse. If the insurers’ preference was not grounded in performance, it may have rested on something else: perhaps the fact that a salaried department, answerable to a city council, could be held to written standards of readiness, whereas a volunteer company’s obligations were matters of custom and honor. Such an explanation would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim, but it would shift its emphasis, locating the decisive change not in the insurance market as such but in a broader preference, shared by insurers and councils alike, for obligations that could be specified and enforced.

Nor does Brandt account for the many smaller towns that kept their volunteer companies well into the twentieth century despite paying higher premiums. Brandt’s account improves on the one she set out to replace; whether it is sufficient depends on how such exceptions are to be explained.

passages.title: Suggestive identifications after Manson v. Brathwaite
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
In the United States, an eyewitness identification produced by a suggestive police procedure—showing the witness a single suspect rather than a lineup, for example, or a lineup in which only the suspect fits the description she gave—is not automatically kept from the jury. In Manson v. Brathwaite (1977), the Supreme Court held that even when a procedure was unnecessarily suggestive, the identification may be admitted if, under the totality of the circumstances, it is reliable. Among the factors courts weigh are the witness’s opportunity to view the offender, her degree of attention, and the level of certainty she demonstrates.

Courts ordinarily learn about these factors from the witness herself, at a hearing months later, and by then the factors may no longer measure what they were meant to. Memory research has established that a witness who receives confirming feedback after choosing someone (“Good, you identified our suspect”) becomes more confident in the choice and, asked later, tends to report a better view and closer attention than witnesses given no such feedback. Such remarks come after the selection and so do not shape it; what they shape is the evidence a court will use to judge it, so that the more a witness has been encouraged, the more reliable her identification may appear. The test thus works like a thermometer that the very fever it is meant to gauge can reset. Some critics conclude that courts should exclude any identification obtained through an unnecessarily suggestive procedure, as a few state courts have done under their own constitutions.

That remedy, however, answers a defect of measurement with a rule about procedure, and the fit is poor in both directions. It would discard identifications that are very likely accurate—that of a witness who, viewing a lineup in which only the suspect fits her description, names him as a coworker she has known for years. And it would leave untouched the confirming remarks that follow a fair lineup, which corrupt the factors just as surely. The difficulty lies less in which procedures courts tolerate than in when they take their measurements.

Suppose instead that police were required to record, at the first identification and before anyone comments on the choice, how confident the witness was and how well she had seen and attended to the offender. Such a record would do little where the procedure itself steers the witness, as when she is shown a single suspect and pushed toward a choice before any confidence can be stated; for procedures of that kind strict exclusion may well be warranted. Elsewhere the record would be fixed before confirming remarks could act on it, and a court could consult it in place of the witness’s later testimony. For the distortion that feedback introduces, a reformed test of this kind, not exclusion, is the proportionate response.

passages.title: Why dispersal persists in crowded habitats
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Many plants equip some of their seeds to travel, on wings, plumes, or hooks, and the traditional explanation is that such equipment carries offspring to newly opened ground, such as a fresh landslip or a fallow field. In stable, fully occupied habitats, however, open ground is rare and most traveling seeds land where they cannot grow. Yet dispersal persists in many of them.

One response keeps the older account and treats these cases as lags: dispersal arose where disturbance was common, and where habitats have since stabilized, selection is stripping it away, though not yet completely. In 1977 the biologists W. D. Hamilton and Robert May proposed instead that dispersal can pay even where no new ground ever appears. A seed that falls beside its parent in a crowded habitat competes chiefly with its own siblings for the few sites that open when occupants die. Suppose a parent drops forty seeds around it and two sites open in a season: at most two of the forty can establish, and a forty-first seed would change nothing but which siblings succeed. A seed carried elsewhere competes mostly with the offspring of other plants, so each one that wins a site adds to the parent’s descendants instead of displacing a sibling. A lineage that sends some seeds away, Hamilton and May showed, should prevail over one that keeps all at home, even if most seeds sent away perish.

Both accounts imply that the share of seeds sent away should fall as the risk to traveling seeds rises, and a study of Crepis sancta, a small annual in the daisy family, bears on it. Each flower head yields heavier, unplumed seeds that drop near the parent and lighter seeds with a plume of hairs that catches the wind. In a city in southern France the species grows in small soil patches around street trees, where a wind-borne seed is considerably less likely than one dropped beside its parent to land on soil. Researchers found that plants from these patches produced a higher proportion of unplumed seeds than did plants from unbroken ground nearby, and that the difference persisted when plants from both sources were raised side by side under uniform conditions.

Since both accounts predict such a shift, it cannot decide between them; they part ways over where the shift should end. Where traveling seeds rarely survive yet sites near the parent remain scarce—a condition the crowded tree patches approximate—the lag account expects dispersal eventually to all but vanish, whereas Hamilton and May expect a substantial share to persist. In the city the unplumed form has gained ground without displacing the plumed one, an outcome consistent with Hamilton and May’s expectation and equally with a population in which selection has not finished its work.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Poets’ recordings of their own work are the best available evidence of how their lines should be timed and stressed, and critics who ignore them misjudge the poems.
Because a poet’s readings of a poem vary from one occasion to the next, recordings of those readings have no legitimate place in the interpretation of poetry.
William Carlos Williams’s recorded readings show that the variable foot, far from being incoherent, is a measure based on duration rather than on syllables.
A poem’s printed form is a more reliable guide to its rhythm than any recording, since poets are often unskilled or nervous readers of their own work.
Although recordings of poets reading their own work can inform interpretation, they capture particular performances and so cannot settle how a poem is meant to sound.
questions.explanation: The author grants that recordings are ‘documents of how a poem was heard’ that can ‘alert us to possibilities,’ but argues across the second and third paragraphs that a reading is one performance of a work that exists apart from it. E says this without the passage’s wording. A is the scholars’ view the author argues against, C is Haverford’s claim, and B and D overshoot: the author gives recordings real evidential value and never ranks the page above every recording.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall claim, with its qualifier.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole passage, especially the first sentence of the second paragraph and the last two sentences of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Whose view is the passage built around, and what does the author do with it? The first paragraph lays out the scholars’ view (recordings are the surest guide). The second and third push back: readings vary, poets aren’t always good readers, the page has its own resources. The last sentence lands it: a recording is evidence, deserving the weight of one performance of a work that exists apart from it. Prephrase: recordings are useful evidence, but they can’t fix how the poem must sound. Watch for answers that give the scholars’ view, or that drop the author’s concession and go too far.

choices.note: The scholars’ view, which is the target of the author’s criticism. The author says the argument ‘asks more of the recordings than they can give.’
Too strong. The author calls recordings evidence that ‘can alert us to possibilities a silent reader might miss.’ That is a legitimate place in interpretation.
This is Haverford’s claim, reported in the first paragraph. The author never endorses it and in fact questions whether the readings reveal any built-in measure.

Tempting, because the author does defend the page and does mention unskilled and uneasy readers. But the author never says the page beats every recording; the claim is that a recording can’t override the page as a verdict, not that it always loses.
CORRECT. It keeps both halves: recordings can inform interpretation (the concession), but they record performances and can’t settle the poem’s sound (the main claim).

questions.stem: The passage mentions which one of the following as a factor that can affect how a poet reads his or her own work in a recording?
choices: the number of syllables in each step of a three-step line
the poet’s discomfort at being recorded
the age and quality of the recording equipment
the indentation the poet chose for the printed lines
the critical reputation of the poem being read
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the second paragraph says ‘unease before a microphone can alter a reading in ways that owe nothing to the verse.’ B restates that. A and D name things the passage does mention, but in other roles: syllable counts come up in Haverford’s claim that each step takes the same time ‘however many syllables it holds,’ and indentation is one of the page’s resources. Tennyson’s phonograph is mentioned, but not as something that changes a reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find something the passage says can change a poet’s recorded reading.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: This is a find-it question, and the interface won’t highlight anything, so you have to know where the author lists things that throw a reading off. That’s the second paragraph: circumstance, poor reading skill, and nerves at the microphone. Prephrase: nerves. The wrong answers that bite are the ones that mention real details from the passage in a different job.

choices.note: Mentioned, but in the wrong role. Haverford says each step of Williams’s line takes the same time however many syllables it holds; syllable count is not said to alter a reading.
CORRECT. ‘Unease before a microphone can alter a reading in ways that owe nothing to the verse.’ Discomfort at being recorded is the same thing.
The passage mentions Tennyson’s Edison phonograph, but never says the equipment changes how the poet reads.
Indentation is one of the page’s resources the poet chose. The passage never says it affects how the poet reads aloud.
Never mentioned. Nothing in the passage ties a poem’s reputation to how it’s read.

questions.stem: By calling the poet’s own voice “the closest thing we have to a score” (fourth sentence of the first paragraph), the scholars most probably mean that a recording by the poet
choices: allows a poem, like a piece of music, to be fully appreciated only by those who have heard it performed aloud
provides a count of the stresses and pauses in each line that the printed text of the poem omits
comes nearer than any other available source to specifying how the poem’s words are to be rendered in sound
must be revised by later readers, as a musical score is by performers, whenever its indications prove inadequate
is consulted chiefly by specialists rather than by the general readers to whom a published poem is addressed
questions.explanation: A musical score tells a performer how a work is to sound; the scholars say print leaves timing open and treat recordings as ‘the surest guide to how the poems should sound.’ C captures ‘closest thing’ (nearest available) and ‘score’ (instructions for sound). A is the tempting overreach: the scholars claim recordings guide how a poem should sound, not that a poem can’t be appreciated without hearing it. B takes ‘score’ in its counting sense.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Translate the metaphor into what the scholars are claiming.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What does a score do? It tells performers how the music should go. ‘Closest thing we have’ means no source gets nearer. So the claim is: the poet’s voice is the best available indication of how the poem should sound. Prephrase: best guide to the poem’s sound. Watch the word ‘score’: one trap takes it as a tally, another stretches the music comparison into a claim about appreciation.

choices.note: Tempting, because it keeps the music comparison. But the scholars never say a poem can only be appreciated by people who heard it. Their claim is about evidence for how the poem should sound.
This reads ‘score’ as a tally. The scholars mean a musical score, a set of directions for performance.
CORRECT. ‘Closest thing we have’ = nearer than any other source; ‘score’ = directions for how the work is to sound.
Nothing in the scholars’ view says the recording should be revised. The point is that it fixes what print leaves open.
The contrast between experts and general readers comes from the author’s third paragraph, and it isn’t what ‘score’ means here.

questions.stem: The author refers to Allen Ginsberg’s readings of “Howl” (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the claim that some poets read their own work in a flat, hurried manner they dislike hearing
suggest that a poet’s later readings of a poem are more authoritative than earlier ones, since they reflect longer acquaintance
show that recordings made before live audiences are less trustworthy than those a poet makes alone in a studio
support the view that because a poet’s performances vary with the occasion, singling out one as the poem’s rhythm is arbitrary
demonstrate that the printed text of “Howl” fails to indicate the rhythm that its author intended the poem to have
questions.explanation: The Ginsberg sentence follows ‘performances answer to circumstance’ and precedes ‘Which of these is the poem’s true rhythm? To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover.’ D gives that role. A names a different point from the same paragraph (unskilled readers), which the Ginsberg example doesn’t illustrate. B and C rank recordings in ways the author never does, and E is the scholars’ kind of claim about the page.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up Ginsberg’s many readings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, second through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the sentence before and the two after. Before: performances answer to circumstance. After: which reading is the true rhythm? Picking one is choosing, not discovering. So Ginsberg is evidence that readings vary, which makes any one reading a choice. Prephrase: to show that a poet’s readings differ, so none can be crowned the poem’s rhythm. Watch for the answer that pulls in the paragraph’s other point (poor readers).

choices.note: Tempting, since it comes from the same paragraph. But the flat, hurried readers are a separate point (‘Nor is a poet necessarily a skilled reader’). Ginsberg is about variation, not poor skill.
The author never ranks later readings above earlier ones. That would be privileging one reading, which is exactly what the author says is a choice.
Live versus studio is never compared. The point is that all the readings differ, not that one kind is worse.
CORRECT. Readings shift with the occasion, so calling any one of them the true rhythm is a choice, not a discovery.
The author doesn’t say anything about the printed text of ‘Howl.’ Faulting the page is the scholars’ kind of argument, not the author’s.

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements about Williams’s recorded readings would the author be most likely to agree?
choices: They show that the critics who dismissed the variable foot as incoherent had misread the printed poems.
They are of little use to anyone seeking to understand how Williams himself conceived of his late poems.
They more probably reflect improvisation at the microphone than any measure Williams had in mind when composing.
They could accurately reflect how Williams chose to read without vindicating his claim about the variable foot.
They are less trustworthy than his printed arrangement of the lines, because he was an unskilled reader of his work.
questions.explanation: The author says Williams’s readings ‘tell us how he chose to perform his late poems’ but that whether they reveal a built-in measure ‘is a separate question.’ D says the same thing in other words: the readings can be accurate records without settling the variable-foot dispute. C is the near-miss: the author says improvisation is ‘at least as plausible,’ not more probable. A is the scholars’ conclusion; B contradicts the author’s point that a reading documents how someone who knew the poem understood it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the author would say about Williams’s recordings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, second through fourth sentences; compare the end of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author actually commit to? Two things: the readings show how Williams chose to perform, and whether they reveal a measure the poems had all along is a separate question. So the author leaves the variable-foot question open. Prephrase: the recordings show his performance choices but don’t settle the measure. Most students who miss this pick (C), because the author does raise improvisation. But ‘at least as plausible’ is a tie, not ‘more probably.’ Watch the strength word.

choices.note: This is Haverford’s conclusion, the view the author questions. The author says whether the readings reveal the poems’ measure is an open question.
Too strong, and it runs against the author’s concession that a reading ‘documents how a poem was understood by someone who knew it intimately.’
Tempting. The author does raise improvisation. But the author says it is ‘at least as plausible’ that the poet improvised, which is a tie, not a judgment that improvisation is more likely.
CORRECT. The readings tell us how Williams chose to perform; whether they reveal a measure the poems had from the start is ‘a separate question.’
The author never says Williams was an unskilled reader. The unskilled-reader point is about ‘some poets’ in general.

questions.stem: The author’s argument in the second paragraph most directly challenges which one of the following assumptions underlying the scholars’ reliance on poets’ recordings?
choices: The rhythm of a poem has some bearing on how the poem ought to be understood by its readers.
The printed page offers a reader no reliable indication of where the stresses in a line of verse should fall.
A measure based on equal spans of time is no less legitimate a basis for verse than one based on syllables.
The way a poet voices a poem on a given occasion reflects the poem itself rather than the circumstances of that occasion.
Recordings that a poet makes late in life deserve more weight than those made when the poems were first written.
questions.explanation: To move from how a poet read a poem to how the poem is built (as Haverford does with Williams), the scholars need a reading to reflect the poem, not the occasion. The second paragraph attacks exactly that: ‘performances answer to circumstance,’ Ginsberg’s readings vary, and unease can alter a reading. That is D. B is the trap: the author does defend the page, but in the third paragraph, not the second, and ‘no reliable indication’ overstates the scholars’ claim that print ‘leaves much of their timing open.’ A is an assumption the author shares.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find an assumption the scholars need that the SECOND paragraph attacks.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph (the scholars’ view, with Williams as their favorite case) and the second paragraph. Check the third paragraph only to rule out the trap.

breakdown.analysis: Two tests: the scholars must rely on it, and the second paragraph must hit it. So what if a poet read a line a certain way, or Williams read each step in equal time? Does that show the poem has that rhythm? Only if a reading is governed by the poem and not by the day, the audience, or the poet’s nerves. The second paragraph attacks just that. Prephrase: a reading reflects the poem, not the circumstances. Most students who miss this pick (B), because the author does defend the page. But that defense is in the third paragraph, and ‘no reliable indication’ is stronger than what the scholars said. Treat the locator in the stem as a hard limit.

choices.note: The scholars do assume rhythm matters, but so does the author. It passes the first test and fails the second.

Tempting. The author does push back on the idea that the page is silent. But that’s the third paragraph (‘the page has resources of its own’), not the second, and the scholars said only that print leaves timing open, not that it gives no reliable indication.
Haverford may need this, but the second paragraph never touches it. The author’s objections are about performances, not about which kinds of measure are legitimate.
CORRECT. The scholars need readings to reflect the poem, and the second paragraph says performances answer to circumstance, vary from occasion to occasion, and can be bent by nerves.
No one compares late and early recordings. Ginsberg’s readings are used to show variation, not to rank them.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: defending the standard explanation of why American cities replaced their volunteer fire companies against a historian’s recent challenge
presenting a historian’s challenge to an accepted explanation and proposing a refinement that would let her account explain every relevant case
assessing a revisionist account of an institutional change, crediting its advantages over its predecessor while noting what it leaves unresolved
arguing that councils’ preference for enforceable obligations, rather than the insurance market, brought about the end of the volunteer companies
contrasting two historians’ explanations of the decline of volunteer fire companies and showing that each is consistent with the evidence
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the standard explanation, presents Brandt’s insurance account with its merits (timing, the volunteers’ support), then names two things it leaves open: why insurers preferred paid departments, and the towns that kept their volunteers. C describes that in general terms. B is the near-miss: the author does sketch a refinement, but it addresses only the insurers’ preference; the holdout towns stay unexplained, and whether the account is sufficient is left open. D turns the author’s tentative ‘perhaps,’ which the author calls compatible with Brandt’s central claim, into a rival thesis.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the passage as a whole is doing.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole passage; the last sentence gives the author’s verdict.

breakdown.analysis: What does the passage spend its time on? One paragraph of background, then Brandt’s account and its merits, then two gaps, then a verdict: it ‘improves on’ the old account, but its sufficiency is still open. Prephrase: evaluating Brandt’s explanation, crediting it and pointing out what it leaves open. Two choices are built to catch you. (B) notices that the author proposes something in the third paragraph and overstates what it accomplishes; (D) notices the councils idea and promotes it to the thesis. Purpose answers are abstract, so expect the key to say ‘a revisionist account of an institutional change’ rather than naming Brandt.

choices.note: Backwards. The author says Brandt’s account ‘improves on the one she set out to replace.’ The author isn’t defending the standard view.

Tempting, because the third paragraph does sketch a refinement. But it only answers why insurers preferred paid departments. The final paragraph says the holdout towns remain unexplained, so no refinement is said to cover every case.

CORRECT. Brandt’s account is weighed: credited for what the standard view couldn’t explain (timing, the volunteers’ support) and faulted for what it leaves open (the insurers’ preference, the holdout towns).

Too strong. The councils idea is offered with ‘perhaps’ and ‘may,’ and the author says it ‘would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim,’ shifting its emphasis rather than replacing the insurance market.
Invents a frame: the standard view isn’t attributed to a second historian, and the author doesn’t find both accounts consistent with the evidence; Brandt’s evidence tells against the standard view.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Brandt cites which one of the following in questioning the standard explanation?
choices: Insurers came to offer lower premiums to cities whose fire protection was provided by a salaried department.
Many smaller towns kept their volunteer companies long after larger cities had replaced them with paid departments.
The volunteers’ reputation for disorder had been established long before cities moved to replace their companies.
A steam fire engine could be operated by a few trained men instead of the many that were needed to work a hand pump.
Prominent members of volunteer companies frequently supported the measures that abolished those companies.
questions.explanation: Brandt’s objections to the standard view are in the second sentence of the second paragraph: many volunteer companies bought steam engines themselves, complaints of rowdiness ‘date from decades before the changeover,’ and losses weren’t greater under volunteers. C restates the rowdiness point. A and E are real parts of Brandt’s argument, but they support her own account rather than counting against the standard one. B is the author’s objection to Brandt, and D is part of the standard explanation itself.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the evidence Brandt uses against the standard explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The standard view has two parts: steam engines and rowdy volunteers. Brandt answers each: volunteers bought steam engines themselves, and the rowdiness complaints were decades old and led to no reform. Prephrase: one of those two points. The traps here are all real details from the passage doing a different job, so check whose argument each one serves.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s Brandt’s claim. But it belongs to her insurance account; it isn’t what she cites against the standard view.
This is the author’s objection to Brandt, in the last paragraph. Wrong party.
CORRECT. Complaints of rowdiness ‘date from decades before the changeover, when they prompted no reform.’ If disorder had been tolerated for decades, it can’t easily explain the timing of the change.
This is part of the standard explanation, not evidence against it.
Tempting. Brandt’s account explains this, as the end of the second paragraph says. But it is offered as a merit of her account, not as a point she raises against the standard view.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the standard explanation has difficulty accounting for which one of the following?
choices: why the steam engine allowed fire companies to work with far fewer members than hand pumps had required
why individual cities replaced their volunteer companies when they did rather than at some earlier time
why rivalries between volunteer companies sometimes ended in brawls at the scene of a fire
why many smaller towns kept their volunteer companies even though doing so raised their insurance premiums
why insurers preferred paid departments even without evidence that those departments fought fires better
questions.explanation: The passage credits Brandt’s account with ‘explaining the timing of the change, which the standard view leaves obscure,’ and Brandt notes that rowdiness had been tolerated for decades. B paraphrases that weakness. D and E are the traps: both are things the author says Brandt’s account fails to explain, not problems raised for the standard view. A and C are ingredients of the standard explanation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage implies the OLD explanation can’t handle.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, especially the sentence beginning ‘Brandt’s account has the merit…’.

breakdown.analysis: Keep the two explanations apart. The author lists two gaps in Brandt’s account (insurers’ preference; holdout towns) and credits Brandt with filling one gap in the standard view: the timing. Prephrase: why the change happened when it did. Most wrong answers here are gaps in the wrong account. Ask, for each choice, whose problem the passage says it is.

choices.note: This is part of what the standard view uses to explain the change. It doesn’t trouble that view.
CORRECT. The passage says the timing is something ‘the standard view leaves obscure,’ and Brandt points out that rowdiness complaints came decades before any reform.
Brawling is one of the standard view’s own premises.
Tempting. This is a problem the passage raises, but for Brandt’s account, in the last paragraph. Wrong account.
Tempting for the same reason. The insurers’ preference is a gap in Brandt’s account (third paragraph). The standard view doesn’t involve insurers at all.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: raise a question Brandt’s account leaves open and suggest an answer that keeps her central claim but relocates the decisive cause
present evidence that undermines Brandt’s claim that changes in the insurance market brought about the end of the volunteer companies
argue that the standard explanation was largely correct after all, since insurers judged that the volunteers fought fires less well
point out a tension in Brandt’s reasoning and conclude that her account must give way to one based on councils’ preference for enforceable duties
explain the procedure by which insurers set premiums and why that procedure favored the cities that maintained salaried departments
questions.explanation: The third paragraph asks why insurers preferred paid departments, notes that Brandt’s treatment of the rate schedules clashes with her own finding about performance, and suggests the preference ‘may have rested on’ enforceable written standards, an idea ‘compatible with Brandt’s central claim’ that would ‘shift its emphasis.’ A says this abstractly. D is the near-miss: the paragraph does point out a tension, but it never concludes that Brandt’s account must give way; it says the alternative is compatible with her central claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the third paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, especially its first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What does the paragraph open with? A question: why did insurers prefer paid departments? Then a tension (Brandt treats the rates as a judgment about performance, yet says volunteers weren’t worse), then a tentative answer (written standards), then how that answer relates to Brandt: compatible, but shifting the emphasis. Prephrase: identify a gap and propose a fix that keeps her main claim. (D) is the trap: it has the tension right and the conclusion wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. The question left open is the insurers’ preference; the suggested answer is ‘compatible with Brandt’s central claim’ but would locate ‘the decisive change’ in a broader preference rather than the insurance market as such.
The paragraph doesn’t attack the insurance claim. The author’s suggestion is explicitly compatible with it.
The paragraph reminds us there is ‘little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse,’ so it doesn’t revive the standard view.
Tempting, because the paragraph does point to a tension in Brandt’s reasoning. But the author never says her account must give way; the alternative ‘would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim.’
Premiums are mentioned, but the paragraph explains no rate-setting procedure; its point is that the reason behind the insurers’ preference is unexplained.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Brandt’s account can most accurately be described as one of
choices: cautious skepticism, since the author grants that it is suggestive but doubts that it is any improvement on the standard explanation
grudging acceptance, since the author concedes its central claim but finds the evidence that Brandt brings against the standard view unconvincing
detached neutrality, since the author reports her evidence without judging whether it supports her explanation better than the standard one
unreserved enthusiasm, since the author regards it as having resolved the questions that the standard explanation had left open
qualified approval, since the author credits it with explaining what the standard view could not but finds some cases still unexplained
questions.explanation: The author says Brandt’s account, if it holds, ‘has the merit’ of explaining the timing, which ‘the standard view leaves obscure,’ and that it ‘improves on the one she set out to replace,’ but says it leaves a question unanswered and that its sufficiency depends on explaining the holdout towns. E captures both the approval and its reason. B is the near-miss: it gets the acceptance of Brandt’s central claim, but its reason is wrong; the author never questions Brandt’s evidence against the standard view and in fact relies on it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize how the author feels about Brandt’s account, and why.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph’s last two sentences, the third paragraph, and the final paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Collect the evaluative words. Positive: ‘has the merit,’ ‘improves on the one she set out to replace.’ Negative: ‘leaves an important question unanswered,’ and sufficiency ‘depends on how such exceptions are to be explained.’ Prephrase: approval with reservations about what remains unexplained. Don’t stop at the adjective; check each choice’s reason against the text.

choices.note: The author says the account ‘improves on the one she set out to replace,’ so the author doesn’t doubt that it is an improvement.

Tempting, because the author does accept Brandt’s central claim. But the reason is wrong, and ‘grudging’ misreads the tone. The author never doubts Brandt’s evidence against the standard view (the steam engines, the early complaints, the fire losses); the third paragraph even uses her ‘little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse’ finding against her.
The author judges plainly: Brandt’s account ‘improves on’ the standard one. Not neutral.
Too positive. The author says the account leaves an important question unanswered and that whether it is sufficient is still open.
CORRECT. Credit for explaining what the standard view left obscure (the timing, the volunteers’ support) plus the reservation that cases like the holdout towns still resist it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the situation that, according to Brandt, led to the disbanding of the volunteer fire companies?
choices: Members of a neighborhood watch disband their group after the city hires more police officers, believing that the group is no longer needed.
A volunteer ambulance corps is replaced by a paid service after a series of widely reported delays in its responses to emergencies.
Farmers vote to close their own cooperative grain store after lenders begin offering cheaper loans to farmers who use licensed commercial storage.
Shopkeepers dissolve their own merchants’ association after a bank begins offering cheaper loans to every local business, whether or not it belongs to an association.
A town council replaces the volunteer lifeguard association at its beach with paid staff after insurers raise the town’s liability premiums, over the objections of the association’s members.
questions.explanation: In Brandt’s account, an outside financial party (insurers) offered better terms to those using a professional alternative, giving the members of a voluntary institution a financial reason to end it themselves. C matches every element: members vote to close their own cooperative because lenders offer cheaper loans tied to the professional alternative. E is the closest miss: insurers drive a shift to paid staff, but over the members’ objections, whereas Brandt stresses that leading volunteers supported abolition. D has a lender’s better terms, but not tied to giving anything up, and B is the standard view’s analogue (a decline in performance).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of Brandt’s explanation, not the subject.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, from ‘What changed, Brandt argues…’ to the end.

breakdown.analysis: Strip Brandt’s story down: 1. members run a voluntary institution; 2. an outside party starts giving better financial terms to people who use a professional replacement; 3. so the members themselves vote to end it. The right answer needs all three. Two choices bring in insurers or lenders, so check the details: is the incentive tied to the professional alternative, and do the members themselves end the institution?

choices.note: Tempting: members end their own group. But the reason is that it’s no longer needed, not that an outside party made ending it financially attractive.
This is the standard view’s logic (performance problems lead to replacement), which Brandt rejects.
CORRECT. Members end their own institution because an outside party (lenders, like insurers) offers cheaper terms to those using the professional alternative.

Close: members end their own group after a lender offers better terms. But the better terms go to everyone regardless, so they give no reason to dissolve the association. In Brandt’s story the discount depends on replacing the volunteers.

Tempting: insurers push a town from volunteers to paid staff. But the members oppose the change. Brandt’s point is that the volunteers’ own leaders, the people with the financial stake, backed ending their companies.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the insurers’ rate schedules discussed in the third paragraph?
choices: They indicate that insurers had better information about local fire losses than city councils had.
They show that insurers judged volunteer companies to fight fires less effectively than paid departments did.
They must have reflected the insurers’ preference for obligations that could be specified and enforced rather than any judgment about performance.
They reflected a judgment by insurers that Brandt’s own findings about fire losses tend to confirm.
Brandt’s interpretation of them sits uneasily with a conclusion she draws elsewhere in her own argument.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Brandt treats the rate schedules ‘as though they simply recorded a judgment about which kind of department fought fires better,’ though ‘she has herself argued that there is little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse.’ So her reading of the schedules is in tension with her own conclusion: E. D reuses the same pieces but reverses their relation; B is Brandt’s reading, which the author questions; and C turns the author’s ‘perhaps’ into ‘must have.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the author would say about the rate schedules.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, second and third sentences; the second paragraph for what the schedules did.

breakdown.analysis: What is the author’s point about the rate schedules? Brandt reads them as a verdict on performance, yet her own research found no evidence that volunteers performed worse. That is an internal tension. Prephrase: Brandt’s reading of the schedules clashes with her own findings. The key says this abstractly (‘sits uneasily with a conclusion she draws elsewhere’). Three traps: (B) is Brandt’s reading, not the author’s; (C) states the author’s tentative suggestion as a certainty; (D) uses the same ingredients and flips the relation between them.

choices.note: The passage says nothing about insurers knowing more than councils.

Wrong party. That is how Brandt treats the schedules, ‘as though they simply recorded a judgment about which kind of department fought fires better.’ The author questions that reading: ‘If the insurers’ preference was not grounded in performance…’

Too strong. The author floats this only as a possibility: the preference ‘may have rested on something else: perhaps’ the enforceability of a salaried department’s duties. ‘Must have’ is far beyond that.

Tempting, because it mentions both the insurers’ judgment and Brandt’s findings on fire losses. But the relation is reversed: she found ‘little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse,’ which undercuts a judgment that paid departments fought fires better.
CORRECT. Brandt treats the schedules as a judgment that paid departments fought better, but ‘she has herself argued that there is little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse.’

questions.stem: Brandt’s criticism of the standard explanation, as described in the second paragraph, most closely conforms to which one of the following principles?
choices: An explanation of a historical change should be rejected if there is even a single case that it cannot account for.
A circumstance cannot explain a reform if it fit the old arrangement or had persisted for years without prompting any reform.
An explanation of an institutional change should identify the parties who stood to gain financially from bringing it about.
A historian should not ascribe a motive to the participants in a historical change unless their own records state that motive.
An explanation that cites economic incentives should be preferred to one that cites technological change or the conduct of those involved.
questions.explanation: Brandt’s objections to the standard explanation are that volunteer companies bought steam engines themselves (so the new engine fit the volunteer system) and that complaints of rowdiness date from decades before the changeover and ‘prompted no reform.’ B generalizes both. C is the trap: it describes Brandt’s own positive account (merchants’ financial interest), not her criticism of the standard view. E names a preference she never states, and A is closer to the author’s later objection to Brandt than to Brandt’s objection to anyone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the general rule behind Brandt’s case against the standard explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, first sentence through ‘nor does she find evidence that fire losses were greater.’

breakdown.analysis: Don’t confuse Brandt’s criticism with her own theory or with the author’s verdict on her. Her criticism: 1. volunteers bought steam engines themselves, so the engine didn’t require paid departments; 2. rowdiness complaints came decades earlier and ‘prompted no reform.’ What rule makes those count against the standard view? A cause that fit the old system, or that sat around for years doing nothing, can’t explain why the change came. Prephrase: a factor that coexisted with the old arrangement without producing change can’t be the explanation. It’s like blaming a breakup on a habit your partner had for ten happy years.

choices.note: Too strong, and the wrong target. Brandt doesn’t point to a single exception; that kind of objection (the holdout towns) is one the author raises against Brandt, and even then the author doesn’t say to reject her account.
CORRECT. The steam engine fit the old arrangement (volunteers bought them), and rowdiness had persisted for decades without prompting reform. Both are reasons such factors can’t explain the change.
Tempting, because Brandt’s own explanation turns on merchants’ financial interest. But that is her positive account, not the basis of her criticism of the standard view.
Brandt’s criticism doesn’t turn on motives stated in records. She uses council minutes to support her own account, not to fault the standard one.
Brandt never argues that economic causes outrank others in general. She rejects the standard factors for specific reasons: timing and compatibility with the old system.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Because suggestion can reshape a witness’s memory, identifications obtained by the police should be kept from the jury unless other evidence corroborates them.
Critics of the Manson v. Brathwaite test are mistaken, because the factors it lists remain a dependable means of judging whether an identification is accurate.
Courts applying Manson v. Brathwaite have given too little weight to a witness’s opportunity to view the offender and too much to the certainty the witness expresses.
The distortion that confirming remarks introduce into the evidence of reliability is better cured by securing that evidence at the outset than by excluding identifications wholesale.
Identifications from procedures that show a witness a single suspect should be excluded, while other suggestive procedures can be cured by recording confidence.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how confirming feedback can inflate the very factors Manson asks courts to weigh, argues that the critics’ remedy of exclusion ‘answers a defect of measurement with a rule about procedure,’ and proposes recording the witness’s confidence at the first identification; for the feedback distortion, ‘a reformed test, not exclusion, is the proportionate response.’ D states that. E is the near-miss: it builds on the concession about single-suspect procedures, where exclusion ‘may well be warranted,’ but that is a side point. B ignores the problem the author accepts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph (the problem), the first sentence of the third, and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Track the shape: a doctrine (paragraph 1), a problem with it (paragraph 2: feedback inflates the factors; critics say exclude), an objection to that remedy (paragraph 3), and the author’s own fix (paragraph 4). Prephrase: the measurement problem is real, but the fix is better timing of the measurement, not exclusion. Check that the key keeps both the problem and the preferred remedy.

choices.note: Too strong, and it adds a corroboration rule the passage never mentions. The author argues against wholesale exclusion.
Backwards. The author accepts that the factors, as courts now learn about them, ‘may no longer measure what they were meant to.’
The passage never weighs opportunity to view against certainty. Its concern is that both can be inflated by feedback.
CORRECT. The problem (confirming remarks distort the reliability evidence) plus the author’s remedy (record that evidence at the first identification rather than exclude).

Tempting, because it echoes the concession in the last paragraph. But the author says only that exclusion for single-suspect procedures ‘may well be warranted,’ a side point, not the passage’s main idea.

questions.stem: According to the passage, under Manson v. Brathwaite a court’s finding that an identification procedure was unnecessarily suggestive
choices: does not by itself determine whether the resulting identification may be presented at trial
requires the court to exclude the identification unless the procedure was necessary in the circumstances
establishes that the identification is unreliable, though the jury may still be permitted to hear it
requires the court to exclude the identification if the witness expresses little certainty about it
permits the identification to be admitted only if the witness knew the offender before the crime
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says that even when a procedure was unnecessarily suggestive, the identification ‘may be admitted if, under the totality of the circumstances, it is reliable.’ So the finding of suggestiveness doesn’t settle admissibility; reliability does. A says this abstractly. B plays on the word ‘unnecessarily’ to invent a necessity test, C wrongly treats suggestiveness as a finding of unreliability, and D turns one factor, certainty, into a decisive one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says follows, under Manson, from a finding of unnecessary suggestiveness.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Under Manson, is a suggestive procedure enough to keep the identification out? No. The court goes on to ask whether it is reliable anyway. So the finding is the start of the inquiry, not the end. Prephrase: the finding alone doesn’t decide admission. The right answer says this in general terms, without the passage’s ‘totality of the circumstances’ wording, so don’t wait for those words.

choices.note: CORRECT. Suggestiveness alone doesn’t settle it; the identification can still come in if it is reliable under the totality of the circumstances.

Tempting, because it plays on ‘unnecessarily suggestive.’ But the passage says that even when a procedure was unnecessarily suggestive, the identification ‘may be admitted’ if reliable. Necessity isn’t the gate.

Half right. The jury may hear it, but not because the identification is deemed unreliable. Manson treats reliability as a separate question that the court decides under the totality of the circumstances.
Certainty is one factor among several weighed under the totality of the circumstances. Nothing in the passage makes low certainty decisive.
Borrowed from the coworker example in the third paragraph, which is the author’s illustration of an accurate identification, not a rule from Manson.

questions.stem: In comparing the test to “a thermometer that the very fever it is meant to gauge can reset” (second paragraph), the author most probably means that
choices: the very influence whose effects the test is meant to assess can alter the measurements on which the test relies
the test yields readings that vary unpredictably from one judge to another even when the facts of two cases are alike
a witness’s memory of the offender deteriorates steadily during the months between the identification and the trial
judges’ own beliefs about a defendant’s guilt can influence how they apply the factors that the test lists
the factors the test lists were chosen without any reliance on research into the workings of memory
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures fever; if the fever could reset the thermometer, the reading would reflect the very thing it is supposed to gauge. The surrounding sentences explain the point: the police influence whose effects the test is meant to assess (the ‘fever’) can, through confirming remarks, inflate the witness’s confidence and reported view and attention (the ‘readings’). A says this in general terms. C is tempting because the passage notes that testimony comes months later, but the metaphor is about the measure being altered by what it measures, not about memory fading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode the metaphor: what is the thermometer, what is the fever?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map it. Thermometer = the test’s reliability factors. Fever = the police influence the test is supposed to assess. ‘Reset’ = confirming remarks inflate the factors, ‘so that the more a witness has been encouraged, the more reliable her identification may appear.’ Prephrase: the thing being measured corrupts the measurement. Look for that structure, in any words.

choices.note: CORRECT. The influence being assessed (the fever) inflates confidence and reported view and attention (the readings) that the test uses to assess it.
Inconsistency between judges is a different problem. The metaphor is about the measure being corrupted by what it measures.
Tempting. The passage does say courts hear from the witness months later. But the metaphor is about influence resetting the gauge, not about memory fading steadily with time.
Judges’ biases never come up. The ‘fever’ is the influence on the witness.
Whether the factors were research-based isn’t the point. The claim is that they can be contaminated, not that they were badly chosen.

questions.stem: The author mentions a witness who names a longtime coworker after viewing a lineup (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that a lineup in which only the suspect fits the witness’s description seldom leads to a mistaken identification
show that suggestive procedures are sometimes necessary if the police are to identify an offender at all
suggest that witnesses who already know an offender are immune to the effects of confirming feedback described in the second paragraph
provide an example of a case in which a court misapplied the factors that Manson v. Brathwaite requires courts to weigh
present a case in which the rule some critics favor would keep from the jury evidence that is very probably sound
questions.explanation: The example follows ‘It would discard identifications that are very likely accurate’: the lineup is suggestive (only the suspect fits the description), so the critics’ exclusion rule would remove an identification that is almost surely right because the witness knows the man. E gives that role. A overgeneralizes from one case: the example shows this identification is likely accurate because of the witness’s prior acquaintance, not that such lineups seldom mislead. C goes too far: the author says the identification is likely accurate, not that such witnesses are immune to feedback.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the coworker example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before the example: exclusion ‘would discard identifications that are very likely accurate,’ then the coworker case. So it is a counterexample to the critics’ remedy. Prephrase: a case where exclusion throws out good evidence. Why is it likely accurate? Not because the lineup was fair (it wasn’t) but because she has known him for years.

choices.note: Tempting, because the example involves that kind of lineup and an accurate result. But the accuracy comes from her long acquaintance with him, and the example is about what exclusion would cost, not about how often such lineups mislead.
The author never says suggestive procedures are necessary.
Too strong. The author says the identification is very likely accurate, not that people who know the offender can’t be influenced by feedback.
No court is described, and nothing is said to be misapplied.
CORRECT. The lineup is suggestive, so the critics’ rule would exclude the identification, though it is almost certainly accurate. That shows the remedy fits poorly.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Recording a witness’s confidence at the moment of the first identification would correct for the effects of every kind of suggestive procedure.
The effects of confirming feedback described in the second paragraph do not arise for witnesses who knew the offender well before the crime.
Identifications made after a witness is shown a single suspect should continue to be assessed by the factors as courts now measure them.
Whether a procedure was unnecessarily suggestive should play no role in deciding whether to admit the resulting identification.
A witness’s confidence as stated before anyone comments on her choice says more about her identification than her later testimony does.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that by the time courts hear from the witness the factors ‘may no longer measure what they were meant to,’ because confirming remarks shape ‘the evidence a court will use’; the fourth proposes a record made ‘before anyone comments on the choice,’ ‘fixed before confirming remarks could act on it,’ to be consulted ‘in place of the witness’s later testimony.’ Together these support E. A contradicts the concession about single-suspect procedures. B is the near-miss: the author treats the coworker identification as likely accurate, but never says feedback leaves such a witness untouched.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author’s claims support, likely by combining two paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, first and third sentences; the fourth paragraph, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase with no topic in the stem, so test each choice against the text. What does the author firmly hold? Later testimony may be inflated by confirming remarks; a record made before anyone comments is fixed before those remarks can act. Put them together: early stated confidence is better evidence than later testimony. Watch for answers that overstate the proposal (‘every kind’) or stretch the coworker example.

choices.note: Contradicted. The author concedes that such a record ‘would not cure every suggestive procedure,’ naming single-suspect procedures.
Tempting. The coworker identification is ‘very likely accurate,’ but that is because she knows him, not because feedback can’t affect her. The author never says the effects don’t arise.
The opposite of the author’s view. For single-suspect procedures the author says ‘strict exclusion may well be warranted.’
Too strong. The author’s reformed test still responds to suggestive procedures; it just uses better evidence of reliability.
CORRECT. Later stated certainty reflects what happened to memory since, while a record made at the moment of choice is fixed before feedback can act and is to be used in place of the later testimony.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author’s claim that, for the distortion introduced by confirming feedback, a reformed test rather than exclusion is the proportionate response?
choices: Witnesses who receive confirming feedback after an identification often recall having had a better view of the offender than they had reported beforehand.
Some witnesses who state their confidence at the moment of identification later remember having expressed much greater confidence than they did.
Witnesses’ first statements of confidence often shift in response to the reactions of an officer who knows which lineup member is the suspect.
Recording a witness’s statement of confidence at the first identification takes little time and requires no equipment that police lack.
A witness who is shown only a single suspect is steered toward that person before she has an opportunity to say how confident she is.
questions.explanation: The reform works only if the record is ‘fixed before confirming remarks could act on it.’ C says an officer’s reactions can shape the witness’s confidence while she is stating it, so the record itself would carry the kind of distortion it was meant to escape. E is the main trap: it restates the author’s concession about single-suspect procedures, a problem the stem’s claim, limited to the feedback distortion, already sets aside. A restates the problem the reform is built to avoid, and B actually supports the reform by showing later memory is unreliable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the author’s case for a reformed test over exclusion.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, especially its second sentence; the second paragraph for the problem the reform addresses.

breakdown.analysis: What does the reform need to be true? The record has to be made before any influence reaches it. So what if influence reaches the witness while she is giving the record? Then the record is contaminated too, and the case for a reformed test over exclusion weakens. Prephrase: something showing that the initial statement itself can be shaped. Most students who miss this pick (E), because it sounds like a problem with the reform. But the stem limits the claim to the feedback distortion, and the author has already conceded single-suspect procedures. A problem outside the claim’s scope doesn’t hurt it.

choices.note: This restates the problem described in the second paragraph. The reform is built to avoid exactly this effect, so it doesn’t undermine the reform.
This actually helps the author. If witnesses misremember what they said, a contemporaneous record is more valuable.
CORRECT. If the officer’s reactions shape the confidence statement as it is being given, the record isn’t fixed before suggestion acts, and the reform fails at its key step.
This makes the reform easier to adopt, which helps the author.
Tempting. It is a real limit of the reform, but the author has already conceded it (‘would not cure every suggestive procedure’), and the claim in the stem concerns only the feedback distortion.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that a long-standing explanation of seed dispersal has been refuted by evidence drawn from a plant growing in an urban environment
set out two explanations of a persistent but seemingly costly trait and assess how far a particular body of evidence can discriminate between them
describe a study showing that the seed dispersal of a plant species changed rapidly in response to conditions in an urban environment
show that two competing accounts of dispersal are each correct for a different kind of habitat and so are not truly in conflict
present a newer explanation of a puzzling pattern and show that a recent study confirms it at the expense of the explanation it replaced
questions.explanation: The passage poses a puzzle (dispersal persists where most traveling seeds die), sets out two explanations (a lag in selection; Hamilton and May’s sibling competition), and then asks how far the Crepis study can decide between them: the shift ‘cannot decide,’ and the persistence of plumed seeds fits both. B describes this abstractly. E is the near-miss: it gets the newer explanation and the study, but the author says the study does not favor it over the lag account. A is too strong for the same reason, and C covers only the third paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the whole passage sets out to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole passage; the first sentence of the last paragraph is the pivot.

breakdown.analysis: Track the moves. Paragraph 1: a puzzle (why disperse where most travelers die?). Paragraph 2: two answers, a lag in selection and Hamilton and May’s sibling competition. Paragraph 3: a study bearing on a prediction both share. Paragraph 4: why the study can’t yet separate them. Prephrase: to lay out rival explanations and weigh whether a piece of evidence settles between them. Watch for answers that let the study crown a winner; the author never does.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says the shift ‘cannot decide between them’ and that the persistence of plumed seeds is consistent equally with an unfinished lag. Nothing is refuted.

CORRECT. The ‘seemingly costly trait’ is dispersal in crowded habitats, the two explanations are the lag account and Hamilton and May’s, and the last paragraph weighs how far the Crepis study separates them.
Half right. The study gets a full paragraph, but it serves as evidence for the larger question of which explanation is right.
The two accounts make different predictions about the same kind of habitat; the passage never assigns them to different habitats.
Tempting: Hamilton and May’s account is newer and the study is recent. But the author says the study cannot decide between the accounts, so it confirms neither at the other’s expense.

questions.stem: The author discusses a parent that drops forty seeds where two sites open (second paragraph) primarily in order to
