choices: illustrate why, where sites are scarce, a plant gains almost nothing from additional seeds that stay beside it
show that a plant in a crowded habitat produces more seeds than can establish themselves and so would do better to produce fewer
show that a seed that stays near its parent competes mostly with the offspring of other plants for open sites
demonstrate that most of the seeds sent away from the parent perish before they reach a site where they can grow
illustrate why the lag account expects dispersal eventually to disappear from habitats in which open ground is rare
questions.explanation: The example shows that with only two sites available, at most two of forty seeds can establish and ‘a forty-first seed would change nothing but which siblings succeed.’ That is the step that makes sending seeds away worthwhile. A says it without the numbers. C reuses the passage’s words but reverses who competes with whom. B draws the wrong lesson (make fewer seeds rather than send some away), and E assigns the example to the wrong account.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the forty-seed example is for.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, third through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What does the example prove? Two sites, forty seeds: at most two succeed, and one more seed just reshuffles which siblings win. So extra seeds kept at home add nothing. That sets up the next sentence: a seed sent away can add a descendant. Prephrase: to show that seeds kept near the parent are largely wasted when sites are few. Watch for the choice that copies the passage’s phrase ‘offspring of other plants’ but attaches it to the wrong seed.

choices.note: CORRECT. With only two sites, more seeds at home only change which siblings win, so they add nothing to the parent’s descendants.

Tempting: the example does show more seeds than sites. But the passage doesn’t conclude that the plant should make fewer seeds; it concludes that some should be sent away, where each that wins a site adds a descendant.
Tempting, because it uses the passage’s words. But it reverses the point: a seed that stays competes with its siblings; it is the seed carried elsewhere that competes with other plants’ offspring.
The example doesn’t concern the seeds sent away. The passage says dispersal pays ‘even if most seeds sent away perish,’ but the forty-seed example isn’t about that.
Wrong party. The forty-seed example belongs to Hamilton and May’s argument that dispersal pays even without open ground; it undercuts, rather than illustrates, the lag account’s expectation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following was found in the study of Crepis sancta?
choices: Plants in the tree patches produced no plumed seeds at all, unlike the plants growing on unbroken ground nearby.
Plants in the tree patches produced heavier unplumed seeds than did plants growing on unbroken ground nearby.
The tree-patch plants’ higher proportion of unplumed seeds was traced to the poorer soil in which they had been growing.
Plants taken from unbroken ground came to produce more unplumed seeds once they were grown in the tree patches.
The city plants’ greater investment in unplumed seeds did not disappear when growing conditions were made the same for all plants.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says city plants produced a higher proportion of unplumed seeds, ‘and that the difference persisted when plants from both sources were raised side by side under uniform conditions.’ E restates that. C is the subtle miss: it explains the difference by growing conditions, which is exactly what the uniform-conditions result tells against. A contradicts the last paragraph, B misapplies ‘heavier,’ and D describes an experiment the passage never reports.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the Crepis study found.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, last two sentences; the last sentence of the passage for A.

breakdown.analysis: Two findings: city plants make a higher share of unplumed seeds, and that difference held up when everything was grown under the same conditions (so it isn’t just a response to the setting). Prephrase: the difference survived uniform growing conditions. Watch for choices that reuse the passage’s words for something the study didn’t find, or that explain the difference away by the setting.

choices.note: Too strong, and contradicted: the unplumed form gained ground ‘without displacing the plumed one.’

Uses the passage’s words (‘heavier, unplumed seeds’) in a new relation. ‘Heavier’ distinguishes unplumed from plumed seeds; the study compared the proportion of each kind, not the weight of seeds between populations.

Tempting, since the patches are small and urban. But the study points the other way: the difference persisted when both groups were grown under uniform conditions, so it wasn’t simply a product of where they had been growing.

Never reported. The plants were raised side by side under uniform conditions, not transplanted into the patches; and the finding was that the difference persisted, not that the country plants changed.
CORRECT. ‘The difference persisted when plants from both sources were raised side by side under uniform conditions.’

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that Hamilton and May’s account, unlike the lag account, would lead one to expect that
choices: plants in recently disturbed habitats should send away a larger share of their seeds than plants in stable habitats do
a seed sent away from its parent is more likely to establish itself than is a seed that falls beside its parent
a plant in a fully occupied habitat could gain from sending seeds away even if no fresh ground ever became available
the share of seeds a plant sends away should fall as the risk faced by traveling seeds increases
plants whose traveling seeds seldom survive should, given enough generations, stop producing such seeds altogether
questions.explanation: Hamilton and May propose that ‘dispersal can pay even where no new ground ever appears’: in a crowded habitat, seeds sent away win sites that would otherwise go to other plants’ offspring. The lag account keeps the older idea that dispersal exists to reach new ground, so in stable habitats it is being stripped away. C captures the difference. D is the trap: Hamilton and May do imply it, but the third paragraph says ‘both accounts imply’ it. E is the lag account’s expectation, not theirs.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a prediction that belongs to Hamilton and May’s account and NOT to the older view.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two paragraphs and the first sentence of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Two filters: Hamilton and May must predict it, and the lag account must not. The lag account ties dispersal to new ground and treats it as fading where ground stays full. Hamilton and May explicitly don’t need new ground. Prephrase: dispersal can pay in a full habitat with no new ground. Most students who miss this pick (D), because Hamilton and May’s reasoning does imply it. But the stem says ‘unlike the lag account,’ and the passage says both accounts imply it. That fails the second filter.

choices.note: If anything this fits the lag account, which ties dispersal to fresh ground. The passage never has Hamilton and May predict it.
Hamilton and May say dispersal pays ‘even if most seeds sent away perish,’ so they need not think a traveling seed is more likely to establish.
CORRECT. They propose that ‘dispersal can pay even where no new ground ever appears,’ whereas the lag account treats dispersal as a means of reaching new ground that is fading where none appears.
Tempting. Hamilton and May’s reasoning does imply this, but ‘both accounts imply’ it. It isn’t a difference.
This is the lag account’s expectation (dispersal should ‘eventually all but vanish’). Hamilton and May expect a substantial share to persist.

questions.stem: Which one of the following findings would, according to the reasoning in the last paragraph, most clearly favor Hamilton and May’s account over the lag account?
choices: In a species whose traveling seeds seldom find open ground, the share of unplumed seeds rises over several generations.
In habitats where landslips frequently open fresh ground, plants send a large share of their seeds away from the parent.
Over many generations in crowded sites where few traveling seeds survive, a population’s share of dispersing seeds falls and then holds steady well above zero.
A plumed species that colonized crowded urban sites only a few decades ago still sends a substantial share of its seeds away, though nearly all of them die.
In crowded sites, a seed that falls beside its parent competes chiefly with its own siblings for the few sites that open.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the accounts ‘part ways over where the shift should end’: where traveling seeds rarely survive and sites stay scarce, the lag account expects dispersal ‘eventually’ to all but vanish, while Hamilton and May expect a substantial share to persist. It adds that persistence is consistent equally with a population in which selection ‘has not finished its work.’ C gives a decline that stops well above zero after many generations, which only Hamilton and May predict. D is the trap: it shows persistence under deadly conditions, but only a few decades in, which is just what an unfinished lag would look like. E states a premise of Hamilton and May’s model that the lag account need not deny.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the finding that separates the two accounts in favor of Hamilton and May.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph, all of it; the first sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author tells you where the accounts differ: not in whether dispersal declines (both say it does) but in where the decline ends. Lag: eventually all but gone. Hamilton and May: a substantial share stays. And the author flags a loophole: a population where selection hasn’t finished looks the same as one that has settled. So the finding must show (1) the deadly, crowded conditions, (2) dispersal that has stopped falling, well above zero, and (3) enough time (many generations) that ‘not finished yet’ is no longer an excuse. Most students who miss this pick (D), because it shows striking persistence under exactly those conditions. But ‘a few decades ago’ is the loophole the author names.

choices.note: Tempting, because it mirrors the Crepis study. But the third paragraph says both accounts imply this decline, so it favors neither.
Both accounts expect heavy dispersal where fresh ground is common. No separation.
CORRECT. Under the conditions where the accounts part ways, the decline stops at a level well above zero, and ‘many generations’ closes the loophole that selection simply hasn’t finished.

Tempting: persistence despite nearly all travelers dying is what Hamilton and May predict. But a recently established population is exactly the case the author says fits equally ‘a population in which selection has not finished its work,’ so it doesn’t favor either.

Tempting, because this is the engine of Hamilton and May’s model. But the lag account doesn’t deny it, and the last paragraph locates the difference between the accounts in where the decline ends, not in who competes with whom.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the result obtained when plants from both sources were raised side by side under uniform conditions (third paragraph) is significant because it indicates that
choices: the difference in seed proportions reflected a difference in the plants themselves, not merely in the settings where they had been growing
plumed seeds released in the tree patches were less likely than unplumed seeds to land on soil
the shift toward unplumed seeds in the city had already reached the point at which, on Hamilton and May’s account, it should end
the city population’s seed proportions favor Hamilton and May’s account over the lag account
plants from unbroken ground would come to produce mostly unplumed seeds if they were moved into the tree patches
questions.explanation: City and country plants differed in their share of unplumed seeds, and ‘the difference persisted’ when both were grown under the same conditions. If the setting alone caused the difference, removing it should have erased it; since it didn’t, the difference lies in the plants, which is what lets the author treat it as the kind of shift both selection-based accounts predict. A says this. B is true of the setting but is background, not what the uniform-conditions result shows. C and D both claim the study bears on where the shift ends or which account is right, which the last paragraph denies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why growing both sets of plants under the same conditions matters.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, last sentence; the first sentence of the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Why would researchers bother growing city and country plants side by side? Picture two kids, one raised on a farm and one in a city, who differ in height. Raise their children in the same house: if the difference persists, it isn’t the house. Same here: if the difference survives uniform conditions, it isn’t the soil patches making the plants act differently; the plants themselves differ. That’s what lets the author treat the result as the shift both accounts (both about selection) predict. Prephrase: the difference is built into the plants, not caused by where they grew. Watch for choices that slide from ‘there was a shift’ to ‘the shift settles the debate.’

choices.note: CORRECT. The difference survived when the setting was held constant, so it lies in the plants rather than merely in their surroundings.
True of the tree patches, but it is part of the setup, not something the side-by-side result shows. Under uniform conditions no seed is landing in a tree patch at all.
Nothing shows where the shift will end; the last paragraph says that is exactly what remains unsettled.
Contradicted. The last paragraph says that since both accounts predict such a shift, the study ‘cannot decide between them.’
Reversed. If anything the result suggests the country plants would not simply switch to the city pattern, since the difference persisted when conditions were the same.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the reasoning by which, according to the passage, Hamilton and May explain the persistence of dispersal?
choices: A baker ships some bread to distant towns though much spoils there unsold, since her neighbors already buy all they want and more loaves at home would only compete with her others.
A farmer whose fields are fully planted buys land in a newly drained marsh, reasoning that the open ground there will let his herds grow faster than they could on his crowded pastures.
A company whose home market is saturated opens branches abroad, reasoning that foreign rivals are weaker and so each branch abroad is likelier to prosper than a new branch at home.
A publisher stops shipping books to distant cities after finding that most copies sent there go unsold, and concentrates its efforts on the bookstores nearest to its warehouse.
A shop owner declines to open a second store on her own street, reasoning that it would mostly take customers from her first store rather than from competitors.
questions.explanation: Hamilton and May’s reasoning: where sites near the parent are saturated, extra seeds kept there only displace siblings, so sending some away adds descendants even if most of those sent away fail. A matches every element: saturated local demand, extra loaves at home only compete with the baker’s own, and distant loaves add sales though much spoils. C is the main trap: it shares the saturated home market, but it justifies going abroad by better odds there, which is not Hamilton and May’s reasoning. E has only the self-competition half, and B is the older account (move to new, open ground).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of Hamilton and May’s reasoning, not its subject.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Spell out the reasoning: 1. the local habitat is full; 2. more offspring at home only displace your own other offspring; 3. so sending some away adds to your total, even if most of those sent away fail. The right answer needs all three, especially the last: the payoff comes from avoiding self-competition, not from better odds away. Two choices match part of it. (E) has the self-competition point but sends nothing away. Most students who miss this pick (C), because ‘saturated home market’ looks like a full habitat. But C’s reason for going abroad is that success is likelier there. Hamilton and May need no such thing; their argument works even when most travelers die.

choices.note: CORRECT. Saturated home demand (full habitat); more loaves at home only compete with her own (siblings displacing siblings); distant loaves add sales though much spoils (dispersal pays even if most travelers die).
This is the older account: go where there is new, open ground. Hamilton and May say dispersal ‘can pay even where no new ground ever appears.’

Tempting: a saturated home market sent abroad. But the reasoning is that each branch abroad is likelier to prosper. Hamilton and May’s reasoning works even when travelers mostly fail; the point is that extra units at home only compete with each other.
This runs the other way: the publisher abandons distant shipments because most fail, which is what the lag account expects selection to do.

Half the structure. It has the self-competition point (a new unit at home only takes from your own), but nothing is sent away to gain elsewhere despite heavy losses, which is the heart of Hamilton and May’s explanation.

questions.stimulus: Apple growers in one valley have noticed something surprising. Apples whose skins develop russeting, a rough brown patch, are generally regarded as blemished, and they fetch lower prices at market. Yet when stored through the winter, russeted apples usually stay free of rot considerably longer than smooth-skinned apples picked from the same trees.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the growers' observation?
choices: Most of the rot that develops in stored apples is caused by fungi that enter the fruit through tiny breaks in its skin.
Smooth-skinned apples that are bruised at harvest rot much sooner in storage than smooth-skinned apples that are not bruised.
Shoppers generally choose smooth-skinned apples over russeted ones even when the two are offered at the same price.
The corky layer of a russet patch slows the entry of the fungi that rot apples.
Russeting is most common in wet springs, and wet weather also encourages the fungi that cause stored apples to rot.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why a supposed blemish goes with fruit that keeps better; D explains it by showing that the russet layer itself protects the apple from rot. A is the near-miss: it says how rot gets in, but nothing says russeted skins have fewer breaks. B compares smooth apples with each other, not with russeted ones. E ties russeting to wet weather, which favors rot, so it deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Russeting is treated as a blemish, but russeted apples resist rot in storage longer than smooth ones.

breakdown.analysis: How can a blemish go along with a better-keeping apple? This is the classic paradox engine: the defect turns out to help. Russeting is bad for how an apple looks and sells, but that doesn't mean it's bad for the apple. We need an answer that shows the russet patch somehow protects the fruit. Watch for answers that explain rot in general, or rot among smooth apples, without tying it to the russet.

choices.note: Tempting, because it gives the mechanism of rot. But it says nothing about russeted skins. A rough, patchy skin could just as well have more tiny breaks than a smooth one. You'd have to add the key fact yourself, and the LSAT doesn't let you.

Tempting, because it explains why some apples rot sooner. But both groups here are smooth-skinned. Unless russeted apples are bruised less often, which we aren't told, the comparison with russeted fruit is untouched.
Shopper taste is the wrong dimension. It explains why russeted apples are seen as blemished, not why they keep longer.
CORRECT. The same change that makes the skin look blemished shields the fruit from rot. A defect in looks, a benefit in storage. Both facts now fit.
Opposite direction. If russeting goes with wet weather, and wet weather favors rot, we'd expect russeted apples to rot sooner. This deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus:
Marisol: The city arts council should stop giving grants to the Brindle Street Theater. Its shows sell out every night, so its ticket sales obviously cover its costs, and grant money should go to companies that cannot pay their own way.

Teodor: Selling out does not mean the Brindle covers its costs. Its auditorium holds only ninety seats, and it deliberately keeps ticket prices low. Without the grant, it would have to raise prices sharply, pricing out many of its regular patrons.
questions.stem: Marisol and Teodor disagree over whether
choices: the Brindle Street Theater's productions are popular enough to fill its auditorium every night
grant money should go to theater companies that cannot pay their own way through ticket sales
the Brindle Street Theater's ticket sales alone bring in enough money to cover all of the theater's costs
a theater company that receives an arts council grant should be expected to keep its ticket prices low
the arts council's grants are what has allowed the Brindle Street Theater to sell out its shows
questions.explanation: Marisol says the sold-out shows mean ticket sales obviously cover the Brindle's costs; Teodor flatly denies that, so C is the point at issue. D is tempting because Teodor values low prices, but Marisol says nothing about ticket prices, so there is no disagreement there.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Marisol: The Brindle sells out, so its ticket sales cover its costs; grants should go to companies that can't pay their way. Teodor: Selling out doesn't mean it covers its costs; with only ninety seats and low prices, it needs the grant.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Marisol: ticket sales cover costs, yes. Teodor's first sentence: no, they don't. That's the clash. Notice what Teodor doesn't attack: Marisol's principle that grants should go to companies that can't pay their way. He may well accept it; he just thinks the Brindle is one of those companies.

choices.note: Both agree. Marisol says it sells out every night; Teodor accepts that and argues from it.
Tempting, but Teodor never rejects this principle. His point is that the Brindle can't pay its way, which fits the principle. No disagreement.
CORRECT. Marisol: yes, ticket sales obviously cover its costs. Teodor: selling out does not mean it covers its costs. Direct yes/no.
Tempting, since Teodor cares about keeping prices low. But Marisol says nothing about ticket prices. One speaker silent means no disagreement we can confirm.
Neither speaker commits to this. Marisol never discusses why the shows sell out, and Teodor talks about what would happen without the grant, not about what caused past sell-outs.

questions.stimulus: Dog owner: Veterinarians routinely urge owners to have their dogs' teeth professionally cleaned every year to prevent gum disease. But my terrier, Biscuit, lived to the age of fifteen without a single cleaning, and his gums stayed healthy to the end. Clearly, the risk that gum disease poses to dogs whose teeth are never cleaned has been greatly exaggerated.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the dog owner's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that annual professional cleanings are the only way to prevent gum disease in dogs
relies on the owner's own impression of Biscuit's gums rather than on a veterinarian's examination of them
fails to consider that some dogs whose teeth are cleaned every year nonetheless develop gum disease
takes for granted that a recommendation made by most experts in a field must be correct
draws a general conclusion about the risk to dogs from a single case that may have been atypical
questions.explanation: One healthy terrier tells us almost nothing about how often uncleaned teeth lead to gum disease in dogs generally, so E names the flaw. B is tempting because a dog owner is no expert, but Biscuit's healthy gums are a stated premise; even granting them, the problem is generalizing from one dog.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The risk of gum disease for dogs whose teeth are never cleaned has been greatly exaggerated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Biscuit never had a cleaning and his gums stayed healthy for fifteen years.

breakdown.analysis: So what if Biscuit was fine? One dog is one dog. Structure: 1. Vets say annual cleanings prevent gum disease. 2. Biscuit had no cleanings and no gum disease. So the risk is exaggerated. That's the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw; it's a classic, know it. It's like saying: my uncle smoked and lived to 90, so the risks of smoking are exaggerated. We need an answer that says the owner generalizes from one possibly lucky case.

choices.note: The owner never claims cleanings are the only prevention. The owner claims the risk without cleanings is small. Different claim.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since Biscuit wasn't cleaned, he must have gotten gum disease, because cleaning is the only way to prevent it.

choices.note: Tempting, because an owner isn't a vet. But the argument states as a premise that Biscuit's gums stayed healthy, and you accept premises. Even if a vet had confirmed it, the conclusion would still rest on one dog.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My cousin says her car's brakes feel fine, so the brakes are safe (no mechanic ever checked them).

choices.note: Irrelevant. If cleaned dogs sometimes get gum disease anyway, that would, if anything, help the owner. It isn't something the argument needed to consider.
choices.example: Example of a real failure to consider: Cleaned dogs rarely get gum disease, so cleaning prevents it (ignoring that owners who pay for cleanings may also feed better diets).

choices.note: Backwards. The owner rejects the experts' recommendation; he certainly doesn't assume they must be right.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most vets recommend yearly cleanings, so yearly cleanings must be necessary.

choices.note: CORRECT. The whole argument rests on one dog. Biscuit might have had unusually good genes or diet. A single case can't show what usually happens to dogs whose teeth are never cleaned.

questions.stimulus: Last year a city water utility began phoning customers in its northern district with an estimated completion time whenever their water service is shut off for repairs. Since then, complaints from northern-district customers about service interruptions have fallen by half, even though interruptions there have been as frequent and as long as before. So the calls, by telling customers what to expect, have made interruptions less frustrating.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Customers in the northern district complain far more often about their water bills than about interruptions in service.
At the same time the calls began, the utility started posting notices of every service interruption on its website for both districts.
Some customers in the northern district say that they usually hang up before hearing the estimated completion time.
Water service interruptions in the northern district are, on average, shorter than those in the utility's southern district.
In the utility's southern district, where customers received no such calls, complaints about interruptions did not decline.
questions.explanation: The argument credits the calls for the drop in complaints, so an answer that rules out a utility-wide cause helps; E shows that the district without calls saw no such drop. D is tempting because it is about interruptions, but it compares the two districts at one time and says nothing about why complaints in the northern district changed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The phone calls made service interruptions less frustrating for northern-district customers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the calls began, interruption complaints in the northern district fell by half; interruptions were as frequent and as long as before.

breakdown.analysis: Complaints dropped after the calls began. But was it the calls? Maybe complaints dropped everywhere, say because the utility made complaining harder or a new billing system put customers in a better mood. To strengthen a before-and-after causal claim, rule out other causes. We need an answer that says complaints didn't fall where there were no calls.

choices.note: Wrong topic. Billing complaints don't tell us why interruption complaints fell.

Tempting as an alternative cause, but it points the wrong way for a strengthener: a new source of information could explain the drop without the calls. And since it covered both districts, it can't be what set the north apart. Either way, it doesn't help the argument.
This slightly weakens the argument: a call nobody listens to can't calm anybody. Wrong direction.

Tempting, since it's about interruptions. But it's a snapshot comparison between districts. The argument is about a change in the northern district over time, and we already know its interruptions didn't change.
CORRECT. This is the comparison group. The district without calls saw no drop, so a utility-wide cause is less likely and the calls look like the difference.

questions.stimulus: Only about 12 percent of one town's registered voters cast ballots in last May's election for the town water board, whereas more than 60 percent voted in last November's election for mayor. Hence, if the water-board election were moved to November and placed on the same ballot as the mayor's race, far more voters would help choose the water board's members.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Most voters who take part in November elections are already well informed about the water board's responsibilities.
Everyone who voted in last May's water-board election would also cast a ballot in a November election.
Turnout in the town's November elections will be at least as high in future years as it was last year.
A substantial number of those who vote in November would not leave the water-board race blank.
Moving the water-board election to November would not increase the overall cost of running the town's elections.
questions.explanation: Showing up to vote is not the same as voting in every race on the ballot; the argument needs D, that many November voters would actually mark a choice for water board. Negate it (nearly all leave it blank) and the plan adds no voters. C is the too-strong trap: turnout could dip a little from 60 percent and still dwarf 12 percent.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Moving the water-board race to the November ballot would mean far more voters help choose the board.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: May water-board turnout was about 12 percent; November mayoral turnout was over 60 percent.

breakdown.analysis: More people would hold the ballot. But would they vote in the water-board race? People who come out for mayor might skip the obscure races further down. The argument quietly treats 'cast a ballot' as 'voted in every race'. We need an answer that says enough November voters would actually fill in the water-board line.

choices.note: Not required. Voters don't have to be well informed to cast a vote. Negated, the argument still stands.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most November voters are well informed about the water board. (They can still vote in the race.)

choices.note: Too strong. If a few May voters skipped November, the total could still rise enormously.
choices.negation: At least one person who voted in May would not vote in November. (Doesn't matter given the size of the gap.)

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. Turnout could fall to 50 percent and still crush 12 percent. The argument survives the negation.
choices.negation: Turnout in future November elections will be somewhat lower than last year's. (Still far above 12 percent.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and almost every November voter leaves the water-board race blank. Then turnout for the ballot rises but participation in the water-board choice doesn't. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Almost none of the November voters would mark a choice in the water-board race.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The conclusion is about how many people vote, not about cost.
choices.negation: Moving the election would increase the cost of running elections. (More voters could still take part.)

questions.stimulus: Conservator: Many museums now remove the overpaint that earlier restorers added to old paintings, on the grounds that it is not the original artist's work. Yet some overpaint is itself centuries old and records how later generations understood the painting. Removing it destroys historical evidence that can never be recovered. Accordingly, although overpaint that hides or harms original paint may need to come off, a museum should not remove old overpaint merely because the original artist did not apply it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the conservator's argument?
choices: Not being the work of the original artist does not, on its own, justify removing a layer of old overpaint.
Overpaint that hides or harms a painting's original paint should be removed, whatever its age or origin.
Many museums now remove the overpaint that earlier restorers added to old paintings, because it is not the artist's work.
Some overpaint is centuries old and records how later generations understood the paintings to which it was added.
Removing overpaint from old paintings destroys historical evidence that, once lost, can never be recovered.
questions.explanation: Everything builds to the last clause: the fact that the artist didn't apply old overpaint doesn't by itself justify taking it off, which A puts in other words. E is the tempting trap; it is a premise supporting that conclusion, and the claim about overpaint that hides or harms original paint is only the conservator's concession.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A museum should not remove old overpaint merely because the original artist didn't apply it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some overpaint is centuries old and records later understanding; removing it destroys unrecoverable evidence.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Sentence 1 is background (what museums do and why). Sentences 2 and 3 are reasons. The last sentence opens with a concession ('although ... may need to come off') and then gives the claim the reasons were for. That final 'should not remove ... merely because' is the conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the final claim, minus the concession, in different words: 'not the original artist's work' is not, by itself, a reason to remove old overpaint. Don't expect the right answer to repeat the stimulus word for word.
This is the concession, and overstated. The conservator grants only that such overpaint 'may need to come off'; it isn't what the argument is trying to prove.
Background. It sets up the practice the conservator is responding to.
A premise. It supports the claim that removal destroys evidence.
Tempting, because it's the strongest-sounding claim. But it's a reason given for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. Ask: does this support the 'should not' claim? Yes. So it's a premise.

questions.stimulus: Many gardeners believe that watering plants in bright midday sun scorches their leaves, because the water droplets focus sunlight like tiny magnifying glasses. In controlled trials, however, droplets on most leaves either spread flat or evaporated before they could focus enough light to do harm. Scorching occurred only on a few species with hairy leaves, whose hairs hold droplets up above the leaf surface. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: water droplets cannot focus sunlight strongly enough to scorch the leaves of any plant in an ordinary garden
gardeners would be wise to avoid watering their plants in bright midday sun, whatever species they happen to grow
plants with hairy leaves suffer more damage from strong midday sun than smooth-leaved plants do, whether or not they are watered
the controlled trials did not reproduce the conditions under which most gardeners actually water their plants
the belief that midday watering scorches leaves holds true for far fewer kinds of plants than many gardeners suppose
questions.explanation: The trials show the scorching effect is real but limited to a few hairy-leaved species, so the popular belief holds for far fewer plants than gardeners think, which is E. B is the trap: it repeats the popular advice that the author is pushing back against, even though the evidence shows midday watering is harmless for most plants.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Many gardeners think midday watering scorches leaves because droplets focus sunlight; 2. in trials, droplets on most leaves spread flat or evaporated before doing harm; 3. scorching happened only on a few hairy-leaved species.

breakdown.analysis: Where is the author going? The first sentence is the popular view. The 'however' signals pushback: on most leaves, nothing happens. But the author also concedes a real effect on a few hairy-leaved plants. So the conclusion should be qualified: the belief isn't baseless, but it covers far fewer plants than people think. Watch for answers that repeat the popular view or swing to the opposite extreme ('never').

choices.note: Too strong. The trials found scorching on a few hairy-leaved species, so 'any plant' contradicts the evidence.
Tempting, because it sounds like sensible caution. But it's the popular view the author is arguing against. For most species the trials found no harm, so 'whatever species' runs the wrong way.
We don't know this. The hairy-leaved plants were scorched because they held droplets up. Nothing is said about sun damage without water.
Unsupported, and it cuts against the author. The argument uses the trials as good evidence; nothing suggests they were unrealistic.
CORRECT. It keeps both halves: the effect is real (hairy-leaved species) but narrow (most leaves are fine). That's exactly where the evidence points.

questions.stimulus: Editor: An author I work with could improve her new biography by adding a chapter on its subject's early career. But researching that chapter would delay publication by at least a year, and the chapter would add little that specialists in the field do not already know. That is why, although the publisher could easily pay for the extra research, I advised against adding the chapter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's reasoning?
choices: An editor should advise against a change to a book only if making the change would delay the book's publication.
An editor should advise against adding material that tells specialists little they do not already know, unless the publisher can easily pay for the research it requires.
An editor should discourage a change to a work whenever what the change would cost is likely to exceed what it would contribute.
An editor should advise against any additional research that the publisher could not readily afford, however valuable the research might be.
An editor should recommend any addition to a book that is likely to improve the book, however slightly.
questions.explanation: The editor weighs the chapter's cost (a year's delay) against its small contribution (little new to specialists) and advises against it; C turns that weighing into a general rule. A gives only a necessary condition for advising against a change, so it permits the advice without requiring it. B's 'unless' clause is triggered here, since the publisher can easily pay, so B says nothing about this case. D's condition isn't met either.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The editor was right to advise against adding the chapter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The chapter would delay publication at least a year; it would add little specialists don't know; money is not an issue.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, using the facts you're given. The facts: a year's delay, little new content, money no problem. The action: advise against the chapter. What is the editor really doing? Weighing what the chapter costs against what it adds. We need a rule like: when a change costs more than it contributes, advise against it. Expect the right answer to say this in general terms, not to repeat 'a year' and 'specialists.'

choices.note: Tempting, because the delay is real and this rule is satisfied. But 'only if' gives a requirement, not a reason. Delay makes advising against the chapter allowed; it doesn't make it right. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

Tempting, because it names the 'little new to specialists' fact. But read the 'unless': the rule tells the editor to advise against such material only when the publisher can't easily pay. Here the publisher can easily pay, so the rule is silent about this case. Unless = if not: if NOT easily paid → advise against. Nothing follows when it is easily paid.
CORRECT. Cost: a year's delay. Contribution: little that specialists don't know. The editor judges the first to exceed the second, and this rule says that's exactly when to discourage the change.
Tempting, because it picks up the stimulus's point about paying for research. But the publisher can easily pay, so the rule's condition isn't met and it says nothing about this case.
Opposite. The chapter would improve the book a little, so this rule would call for recommending it.

questions.stimulus: In a recent study, people who described themselves as habitual procrastinators kept a daily diary for a month, noting each task they put off and how they felt each evening. On 70 percent of the days on which they put off an important task, they reported feeling anxious that evening. This shows that putting off important tasks tends to make habitual procrastinators anxious.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about people in general from a study limited to those who call themselves habitual procrastinators
fails to consider how often the participants felt anxious on days when they put off nothing important
takes for granted that the participants put off unimportant tasks less often than they put off important ones
relies on the participants' own reports of how they felt rather than on an independent measure of their anxiety
presumes, without providing justification, that the participants were right to describe themselves as habitual procrastinators
questions.explanation: Seventy percent means nothing without a baseline: if the participants felt anxious on 70 percent of all their evenings, procrastinating made no difference, so B names the missing comparison. A is tempting but misreads the conclusion, which is limited to habitual procrastinators, the very group studied.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Putting off important tasks tends to make habitual procrastinators anxious.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On 70 percent of the days they put off an important task, participants reported anxiety that evening.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent sounds high. High compared to what? If these people feel anxious on 70 percent of all evenings, procrastination changes nothing. This is the missing comparison group: the study reports what happened on procrastination days only. It's like saying a lucky sweater works because your team won 70 percent of the games you wore it, without checking how often they win when you don't. We need an answer that points to the non-procrastination days.

choices.note: Tempting at a glance, but read the conclusion: it's about habitual procrastinators only, the same group studied. No leap to people in general.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Habitual procrastinators get anxious when they delay tasks, so everyone does.

choices.note: CORRECT. Without the anxiety rate on other days, 70 percent has no baseline. If they're anxious 70 percent of the time anyway, procrastinating makes no difference.
Irrelevant. Unimportant tasks never enter the argument, and nothing depends on how often they're delayed.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since procrastinators delay important tasks, they must delay trivial ones even more.

choices.note: Tempting, since self-reports can be shaky. But anxiety is a feeling, and asking people is a reasonable way to measure it. Even with a perfect measure, the 70 percent would still have no baseline.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Patients said they felt calmer after the drug, so their blood pressure must have dropped.

choices.note: So? If a few participants weren't 'true' procrastinators, the core problem remains. This is a nitpick about labels, not the gap.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our survey respondents call themselves early risers, so they must wake before six.

questions.stimulus: Councilor: Some residents propose that only people who have lived in our town for at least ten years be allowed to serve on its planning commission, on the grounds that long residence ensures familiarity with the town's needs. But length of residence is a poor test of such familiarity. Under the proposed rule, the engineer who designed the town's flood-control system, who moved here six years ago and knows the town's drainage better than anyone, would be barred from serving.
questions.stem: The claim that the engineer who designed the town's flood-control system would be barred from serving plays which one of the following roles in the councilor's argument?
choices: It describes an implication of the residents' proposed test that the councilor treats as showing the test to be flawed.
It is offered as an illustration of the residents' claim that long residence ensures familiarity with the town's needs.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the engineer should be appointed to the planning commission.
It is offered as evidence that the residents' proposal, though sound in principle, would be difficult to enforce in practice.
It is the argument's main conclusion, and the claim about the engineer's knowledge of drainage is offered in support of it.
questions.explanation: The councilor applies the residents' ten-year rule, gets a result that looks absurd (the person who knows the drainage best is barred), and uses that result to discredit the rule; A describes this abstractly. C is the near-miss: the claim is a premise, but it supports the conclusion about length of residence, not any claim about appointing the engineer. D is tempting because the claim counts against the proposal, but the point is that the rule gives the wrong answer, not that it is hard to enforce.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Length of residence is a poor test of familiarity with the town's needs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Under the ten-year rule, the flood-control engineer, who knows the town's drainage best, would be barred.

breakdown.analysis: There's no 'so' or 'therefore' here; the conclusion sits in the middle ('But length of residence is a poor test of such familiarity') and the last sentence backs it up. The councilor takes the residents' rule, applies it, and gets a result that looks absurd: the person who knows the drainage best can't serve. The councilor doesn't like this outcome. It's the absurd result used to sink the rule. The claim supports the conclusion, so it's a premise, but a specific kind: a consequence the councilor rejects.

choices.note: CORRECT. The engineer's exclusion follows from the residents' test, and the councilor treats it as a result no sensible test would produce, so the test must be flawed. 'Implication' is the hypothetical consequence; 'showing the test to be flawed' is how it's used.
Opposite relation. The example counts against the residents' claim that long residence ensures familiarity, not for it.

Tempting: the claim is a premise. But a premise for what? The councilor never argues that the engineer should be appointed. The conclusion is that length of residence is a poor test. Right role, wrong target.

Tempting, because the example does count against the proposal. But it's about the rule giving a bad result, not about enforcement. Nothing suggests the rule would be hard to apply; it applies all too easily. And the councilor doesn't call the proposal sound in principle.

No. The conclusion is the unflagged second sentence: length of residence is a poor test. The engineer's exclusion supports that conclusion; it isn't the conclusion. Don't assume the conclusion comes last.

questions.stimulus: The striped blenny, a small reef fish, often bobs its head rapidly when another blenny approaches. Male blennies do this far more often than females do, and only males defend territories on the reef. So the head-bobbing is probably a warning that males use to drive rivals away from their territories.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Male blennies bob their heads far more often when a female approaches than when a male does.
Male blennies that lose their territories to rivals stop bobbing their heads within a few days of the loss.
Some males that bob their heads at approaching rivals nonetheless lose their territories to those rivals.
Several other reef fish species defend their territories without making any head movements at all.
Females that approach a male's territory are seldom driven away, whether or not the male bobs his head at them.
questions.explanation: If males bob mostly at approaching females, the display looks like courtship rather than a warning to rivals, so A undercuts the proposed function. B is tempting because it ties bobbing to territory, but that link supports the argument. C is a near-miss: a warning that sometimes fails is still a warning.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Head-bobbing is probably a male's warning to drive rivals from his territory.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Blennies bob when another approaches; males bob far more than females; only males hold territories.

breakdown.analysis: The argument guesses a function from who does it. But males do lots of things females don't, like courting. Maybe the bob is about attracting mates, not repelling rivals. When an argument guesses what a trait is for, weaken it with a different job the trait could be doing. We need an answer that points to another function, ideally tied to who the bob is aimed at.

choices.note: CORRECT. If males bob mostly at females, the bob looks like a courtship signal. A warning to rivals should be aimed at rival males.
Tempting, since it mentions territory. But it strengthens the argument: no territory, no bobbing, which fits a territorial warning. Wrong direction.
Tempting, because it ties bobbing to rivals and territory. But a warning that sometimes fails is still a warning. Nothing here suggests the bob serves some other purpose.
So? Other species defending territories some other way says nothing about what this blenny's bob is for.

Tempting, because it reuses 'driven away' and seems to show the bob doesn't repel. But the argument says the bob is meant for rivals, and females aren't rivals. A warning that doesn't drive off non-rivals fits the argument fine.

questions.stimulus: Under Penner Marina's rules, a boat may leave the marina only if its bilge pump has been tested that day, and only staff members who hold a current safety certificate may test bilge pumps. Any boat carrying paying passengers must also have a licensed pilot aboard, unless it is a water taxi bound for Gull Island. Today every boat obeyed these rules, and the Wren, which is carrying paying passengers, left the marina with no licensed pilot aboard.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Today a staff member with a current safety certificate tested the bilge pump of a water taxi bound for Gull Island.
Every water taxi that left the marina today for Gull Island did so without a licensed pilot aboard.
Any boat that left the marina today with a licensed pilot aboard was carrying paying passengers.
A water taxi bound for Gull Island may leave the marina even if its bilge pump has not been tested that day.
No boat other than the Wren left the marina today without a licensed pilot aboard.
questions.explanation: Two chains meet in the Wren. It left, so its pump was tested today by a certified staff member; it carried paying passengers with no pilot, so it must be a water taxi bound for Gull Island. A combines both without naming the Wren. D is the trap: the water-taxi exception covers only the pilot rule, not the pump test.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Leaves marina → pump tested that day; 2. Pump tested → by a certified staff member; 3. Paying passengers AND no licensed pilot → water taxi bound for Gull Island (contrapositive of the pilot rule); 4. Every boat obeyed the rules today; 5. The Wren carried paying passengers, had no pilot, and left.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase with five rules, so chain what you know about the Wren. Chain 1: Wren left → pump tested today → tested by certified staff. Chain 2: the pilot rule says paying passengers → pilot, unless water taxi to Gull Island. The Wren had passengers and no pilot, yet obeyed the rules, so it must be the exception: a Gull Island water taxi. Put the chains together: a certified staff member tested the pump of a Gull Island water taxi today. Watch for answers that stretch the exception beyond the pilot rule, reverse an arrow, or say something about boats other than the Wren.

choices.note: CORRECT. The Wren is that water taxi. It left, so its pump was tested today, and only certified staff can test pumps. The answer hides the Wren behind a description, which is why it's easy to skip.
We don't know this. The Wren is one such taxi, but others could have carried pilots; the exception permits going without a pilot, it doesn't require it.
This reverses the pilot rule. Passengers → pilot (with the exception), not pilot → passengers. A boat with no passengers could carry a pilot anyway.
Tempting, because water taxis do get an exception. But the exception is attached only to the pilot rule. Every boat that leaves needs a tested pump, taxis included. This contradicts the rules.
We don't know this. Other water taxis, or boats with no paying passengers, could also have left without a pilot.

questions.stimulus: Surveys in one city show that residents of neighborhoods with a full-service grocery store eat considerably more fresh fruit and vegetables than residents of neighborhoods without one. Yet when new full-service grocery stores opened in several of the city's neighborhoods that had lacked them, residents' consumption of fruit and vegetables there did not rise over the following three years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Fruit and vegetables at the city's full-service grocery stores cost more, on average, than the same items do at corner shops.
Before the new stores opened, many residents of those neighborhoods said they would buy more produce if a store were nearby.
People who care most about eating fresh produce tend to move to neighborhoods that already have full-service grocery stores.
Residents of neighborhoods with full-service grocery stores also tend to eat less fast food than other city residents typically do.
The new grocery stores are larger, on average, than the full-service stores in the city's other neighborhoods.
questions.explanation: If people who care about eating produce choose to live where stores already are, the first fact reflects who lives near stores, not what stores do to residents, so a new store need not change anyone's diet; that is C. A is tempting because it gives a reason residents might not buy produce at the new stores, but it leaves unexplained why residents near the existing stores eat more.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: People who live near full-service grocery stores eat more produce, but opening new stores didn't raise produce eating in the neighborhoods that got them.

breakdown.analysis: If stores make people eat more produce, new stores should have worked. They didn't. So maybe the store isn't the cause of the first pattern at all. Who lives near stores? Maybe the produce lovers moved there. That's a self-selection explanation, and it lets both facts be true. We need an answer that says the link in fact 1 comes from who chooses to live where, not from the store.

choices.note: Tempting, because it gives a reason the new stores might not change buying. But it explains only one side. If store produce is pricier, why do residents near the existing stores eat more? The first fact is left hanging.
This deepens the puzzle. Residents said they'd buy more, and then didn't.
CORRECT. Fact 1 then reflects who chooses to live near stores, not an effect of the stores. A new store doesn't change the diets of the people already living there, so fact 2 fits too.
So? Another difference between the groups doesn't explain why new stores changed nothing.
If anything, bigger stores should have helped more. This doesn't resolve anything.

questions.stimulus: Economic historian: About two hundred letters written by merchants of the port of Edrin during the 1780s survive today, and nearly three-quarters of them complain about the condition of the roads leading inland from the port. Evidently, most of Edrin's merchants in that decade regarded those roads as a serious obstacle to their trade.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economic historian's argument depends?
choices: Letters complaining about the inland roads were not much more likely than the merchants' other letters to have been preserved.
Every merchant who did business in Edrin during the 1780s wrote at least one of the letters that survive today.
The roads leading inland from Edrin were in worse condition during the 1780s than they were in any later decade.
Merchants who complained about the roads in their letters also raised their complaints with the port's officials.
Most of the surviving letters were written by merchants whose trade depended on moving goods inland.
questions.explanation: The historian generalizes from the letters that happen to survive to all of Edrin's merchants, so the surviving letters must not overrepresent complaints; A says complaint letters weren't much likelier to be kept. Negate it and the three-quarters figure could reflect what got saved, not what merchants thought. B is the too-strong trap: the sample doesn't need to include every merchant to be representative.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Edrin merchants in the 1780s saw the inland roads as a serious obstacle to trade.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: About three-quarters of the roughly two hundred surviving merchant letters from the 1780s complain about those roads.

breakdown.analysis: Which letters survive? Not a random draw. If letters about the roads were filed away by officials, or kept because they mattered in some later dispute, while routine letters were thrown out, then the survivors would be stacked with complaints. It's like judging a restaurant by the reviews pinned to the complaints board. This is a sampling argument, and the sample is whatever happened to be preserved. We need an answer that says the surviving letters aren't skewed toward road complaints.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: complaint letters were much more likely to be preserved. Then the surviving pile overstates how common complaints were, and the jump to 'most merchants' collapses.
choices.negation: Letters complaining about the inland roads were much more likely than other letters to have been preserved.

choices.note: Too strong. The surviving letters could be a fair sample even if many merchants wrote none of them. Negated, the argument still stands.
choices.negation: At least one Edrin merchant of the 1780s wrote none of the surviving letters. (A sample needn't include everyone.)

choices.note: Not required. The merchants could think the roads were a serious obstacle whether or not later decades were better or worse.
choices.negation: In some later decade the roads were in at least as bad condition as in the 1780s. (No effect on what 1780s merchants thought.)

choices.note: Out of scope. The argument is about what merchants thought, not whether they took it to officials.
choices.negation: Some merchants who complained in letters never raised it with officials. (They can still have seen the roads as a problem.)

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties the letter-writers to inland trade, which seems to explain their complaints. But negate it: most letters came from merchants who didn't depend on inland routes. Then complaints are, if anything, even more widespread. The argument doesn't need this.
choices.negation: Most of the surviving letters were written by merchants whose trade did not depend on moving goods inland. (The argument survives.)

questions.stimulus: Every pond included in a wetland survey is either spring-fed or rain-fed. All of the spring-fed ponds in the survey stay free of ice throughout the winter, and each surveyed pond that stays free of ice throughout the winter was found to hold a breeding population of palmate newts. Some of the rain-fed ponds in the survey, however, hold no newts at all.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: Some of the rain-fed ponds in the survey stay free of ice throughout the winter.
Every pond in the survey that holds a breeding population of palmate newts is spring-fed.
None of the surveyed ponds that lack newts stays free of ice throughout the winter.
Not every spring-fed pond in the survey was found to hold a breeding population of palmate newts.
Most of the ponds in the survey freeze over at some point during the winter.
questions.explanation: Spring-fed → ice-free → breeding newts, so every spring-fed pond holds breeding newts, and D, which says not every one does, contradicts the chain. B is the reversal trap: the chain runs from spring-fed to newts, not back, but a pond with newts happening to be spring-fed is still possible. C must be true, so it can't be the answer to a CANNOT question.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every surveyed pond is spring-fed or rain-fed; 2. Spring-fed → ice-free all winter; 3. Ice-free all winter → breeding palmate newts; 4. Some rain-fed ponds have no newts.

breakdown.analysis: A CANNOT-be-true question: four answers could be true (or must be true), and one contradicts the facts. Chain it: spring-fed → ice-free → breeding newts. So every spring-fed pond has breeding newts. Contrapositive: no breeding newts → not ice-free → not spring-fed. Look for an answer that breaks the chain. It may be dressed up as a negation ('not every').

choices.note: Could be true. Nothing says only spring-fed ponds stay ice-free. Some rain-fed ponds could be ice-free (and would then have newts, which is consistent, since only some rain-fed ponds lack them).

Tempting, because it flips the chain into something that looks forbidden or required. But it can be true: if every newt pond happens to be spring-fed, nothing in the facts is violated. A reversal isn't required, but it isn't ruled out either.
This must be true (contrapositive: no newts → not ice-free), so it certainly can be true. A trap for anyone who hunts for the answer that 'follows.'
CORRECT. 'Not every spring-fed pond has breeding newts' means some spring-fed pond lacks them. But spring-fed → ice-free → breeding newts. That's a contradiction, so this cannot be true.
Could be true. Rain-fed ponds needn't stay ice-free, and we don't know how many ponds are rain-fed. Most could freeze.

questions.stimulus: On a certain mountain rail line, broken rails are reported far more often in winter than in summer. Some attribute this to the heavier freight traffic of the winter months. But only the line's eastern section carries more freight in winter, and the winter rise in breaks is about as large on the western section as on the eastern. The cold, which makes steel rails contract and puts them under tension, is therefore the more likely cause.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: On the line's western section, more passenger trains run in winter than in summer, carrying skiers to resorts along the route.
Freight trains on the line's eastern section are heavier in winter because they carry heating oil to towns along the route.
Breaks on both sections of the line most often occur at welds, where small flaws in the steel are most common.
Steel rails expand in summer heat, and on some lines that expansion damages track more often than winter contraction does.
Rails laid in cold weather, which are under less tension when winter temperatures drop, show a much smaller winter rise in breaks.
questions.explanation: The argument rules out freight by noting that the western section gets the same winter rise without extra freight. E tests the proposed mechanism directly: rails that the cold puts under less tension (those laid in cold weather) show much less of a winter rise, though they carry the same trains. That dose-response link favors cold-induced tension. A is the trap that runs the other way: winter passenger traffic in the west could explain the western rise without the cold, so it weakens. C reuses 'small flaws' but fits either cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Cold contraction, not heavier freight, is the more likely cause of the line's winter rail breaks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only the eastern section gets more winter freight, yet the winter rise in breaks is about as large on the western section.

breakdown.analysis: The author has already done half the work: the western section shows the winter rise without extra freight, so freight can't be the whole story. What's left open? Maybe something else about winter, besides cold, hits the west. A good strengthener ties the breaks to the specific mechanism named: cold → contraction → tension → breaks. If that's right, rails that end up under less tension in the cold should break less in winter, while carrying the same traffic. Don't wait for an answer that simply says 'the cold.' Most students pick (A) or (C). (A) looks like it's about traffic, which the author dismissed, but it actually hands the western section a new non-cold cause, so it weakens. (C) borrows 'small flaws' from the mechanism but fits freight just as well. The right answer talks about when rails were laid, which looks off-topic until you connect it to tension.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about traffic, which the argument already dismissed. But it gives the western section its own winter traffic increase, which could explain the western rise without the cold. That weakens the argument.
Irrelevant. Why eastern freight is heavier in winter doesn't bear on whether freight or cold causes the breaks.
Tempting, because it echoes the 'small flaws' in the mechanism. But flaws at welds could be opened by heavy loads or by contraction. It doesn't favor either cause.
True-sounding but beside the point. Other lines and summer damage say nothing about what causes this line's winter breaks.

CORRECT. Rails laid in cold weather are under less tension in winter, and they show a much smaller winter rise, even though they carry the same trains on the same sections. Less tension, fewer winter breaks: that's exactly what the cold-tension explanation predicts and what the freight explanation doesn't.

questions.stimulus: Runner: The organizers of this year's city marathon allowed two entrants who were injured in training to defer their paid entries to next year's race. I too was injured in training, as seriously as they were and at the same point before the race, yet my request to defer was refused. Since the organizers are obligated to treat entrants in the same situation alike, they must let me defer my entry as well.
questions.stem: The runner's argument is flawed because it
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that the two other entrants' injuries were as serious as the runner's own injury
draws a general conclusion about how all marathon organizers should behave from the conduct of one race's organizers
treats the organizers' refusal as evidence that they favored the two other entrants for reasons unrelated to their injuries
treats one way of removing an inconsistency in how people have been treated as though it were the only way
fails to consider that the runner might be able to sell or transfer the entry to another runner instead
questions.explanation: The organizers have treated like entrants differently, but consistency can be restored either by granting the runner's deferral or by revoking the other two; (D) describes this abstractly as treating one way of removing an inconsistency as the only way. (A) is the dominant trap: it questions whether the cases are alike, but the runner states that as a premise. (C) describes a motive the runner never alleges.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The organizers must let the runner defer the entry.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Organizers must treat entrants in the same situation alike; two injured entrants were allowed to defer; the runner was injured just as seriously, at the same point, and was refused.

breakdown.analysis: Does treating like cases alike require saying yes to the runner? Not necessarily. Right now the organizers have treated three like entrants differently: two got a yes, one got a no. Consistency can be restored two ways: grant the runner a deferral too, or take back the other two. The runner assumes the only fix is the one the runner wants. It's like a child saying, 'You let my brother stay up late, so to be fair you have to let me stay up too.' A parent could be just as fair by sending the brother to bed. We need an answer that points to the other way of being consistent. Most students pick (A), because 'maybe their situations differ' is the standard objection to a fairness argument. But the runner states outright that the injuries were as serious and came at the same point. That's a premise, and the LSAT asks you to accept premises; a flaw answer has to describe the move from premises to conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'maybe the cases differ' is the usual way to attack a fairness argument. But the runner says outright that the injuries were equally serious; that's a premise, and you accept premises. The problem is what the runner concludes from them.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My neighbor got a permit for a fence, so I should get one too (with nothing said about whether the two yards are alike).

choices.note: No generalization happens. The runner draws a conclusion only about this race's organizers and this one request.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: This race's organizers grant deferrals, so every marathon in the country should grant them.

choices.note: The runner never claims favoritism. The argument rests only on the duty to treat like cases alike, whatever the organizers' reasons for the difference.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: They turned me down, so they must have been playing favorites with the others.

choices.note: CORRECT. The inconsistency: two like entrants got deferrals and the runner didn't. Two ways to remove it: defer the runner, or revoke the others. The runner treats the first as the only option. The abstract wording ('one way of removing an inconsistency') is why it's easy to skip.

Tempting in a small way, because it also points to an option the runner ignores. But selling the entry has nothing to do with what equal treatment requires of the organizers, which is the only thing the conclusion rests on.

questions.stimulus: According to a principle that many museums follow, a museum should lend a work from its collection to another institution only if the borrower guarantees climate-controlled display. Moreover, unless a conservator has examined the work within the past year, the museum should lend it only for a period of three months or less.
questions.stem: The principle stated above, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: The museum should lend its bronze horse for a two-month show at a university gallery that guarantees climate-controlled display, since the bronze has never needed conservation.
The museum should not lend its tapestry for a six-month exhibition at a gallery that guarantees climate-controlled display, since no conservator has examined the tapestry in two years.
The museum should not lend its altarpiece for a ten-week exhibition at a gallery with climate-controlled display, since no conservator has examined the altarpiece in the past year.
The museum should not lend its sketchbook for a five-month exhibition at a climate-controlled library, since the library has never before borrowed a work from the museum.
The museum should lend its portrait for a year-long exhibition, since a conservator examined it four months ago and the borrower guarantees climate-controlled display.
questions.explanation: The principle gives only necessary conditions for lending: a climate-control guarantee, and either a conservator's examination within the past year or a loan of three months or less. So it can justify only refusals, and only where a condition fails. B's tapestry fails both halves of the second condition (no recent examination, six-month loan), so refusal is justified. E is the dominant trap: it meets every condition, but meeting necessary conditions doesn't make lending required. C misreads the 'unless' clause: a ten-week loan is allowed even without an examination.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Lend → borrower guarantees climate control. Lend AND not examined within past year → loan is 3 months or less. (Equivalently: lend → examined within a year OR loan ≤ 3 months.)

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the argument whose conclusion the principle actually establishes.

breakdown.analysis: Both rules are 'only if' rules, so they tell you when NOT to lend, never when you must lend. That kills every positive conclusion at once, however well the facts line up. For a 'should not lend' conclusion, you need a case that fails a condition: no climate guarantee, or (no examination within a year AND a loan longer than three months). Check each refusal against both parts. Most students pick (E), because the portrait ticks every box. But ticking the boxes of an 'only if' rule makes lending permitted, not required. And watch the 'unless': a short loan is fine even without an examination.

choices.note: A positive conclusion. The principle only says when not to lend, so it can't establish that the museum should lend. Also, 'never needed conservation' isn't the same as 'examined by a conservator.'
CORRECT. Climate control is guaranteed, but the tapestry hasn't been examined within the past year, so the loan must be three months or less. Six months fails. The principle says not to lend.
Tempting, because the altarpiece hasn't been examined within the year. But that only caps the loan at three months, and ten weeks is under three months. Nothing in the principle forbids this loan.
The reason given (no borrowing history) isn't part of the principle. And we don't know whether the sketchbook was examined recently, so we can't tell whether the five-month loan fails a condition.
Tempting: every condition is met. But the principle states necessary conditions for lending, not sufficient ones. Meeting them means lending isn't ruled out; it doesn't mean the museum should lend.

questions.stimulus: Every taxpayer in one province recently answered a survey about provincial taxes. Most of the respondents said that they believe they pay a larger share of their income in provincial taxes than most other taxpayers in the province do. Many respondents also said that provincial taxes are too high and that the burden is unfairly distributed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Most taxpayers in the province are mistaken about how the share of their income that they pay in provincial taxes compares with others' shares.
The province's taxes place a heavier burden on most taxpayers than those taxpayers themselves believe.
The taxpayers in the province who pay the largest share of their income in provincial taxes are the most likely to call those taxes too high.
Not every taxpayer in the province who believes that his or her provincial tax share is larger than most others' shares is correct.
Most taxpayers in the province pay a smaller share of their income in provincial taxes than they believe they pay.
questions.explanation: It is impossible for most taxpayers to pay a larger share than most others, so some of those who believe they do must be wrong; (D) states this as 'not every taxpayer who believes it is correct.' (A) is the dominant trap: if, say, 60 percent hold the belief and about half really are above the middle, only around 10 percent need be mistaken, far short of most.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every taxpayer in the province answered; 2. most believe they pay a larger share of income in provincial taxes than most other taxpayers in the province; 3. many think taxes are too high and unfairly distributed.

breakdown.analysis: Can most people really pay more than most others? No. To pay more than most others, you have to be above the middle, and at most about half the people can be above the middle. So if more than half believe they're above the middle, some of them must be wrong. But only some. Imagine 100 taxpayers: 60 believe they're in the top half, and the top half really holds 50. At least 10 are wrong. Ten is not most. Watch the subset trap: 'some are mistaken' follows; 'most are mistaken' doesn't. Most students pick (A), because the belief is so widespread that it feels like most people must be wrong. The numbers above show they needn't be. The right answer hides as a double negative: 'not every believer is correct' is just 'some believers are wrong' in disguise.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's the classic trap. The numbers force only some mistakes, not most. With 60 believers and 50 real top-halfers, as few as 10 need be wrong.
