Wrong direction and unsupported. If anything, the mistaken ones think their burden is relatively larger than it is.
We don't know this. The stimulus never links actual tax share to opinions about whether taxes are too high.
CORRECT. 'Not every believer is correct' = 'at least one believer is wrong.' Since most believe they're above most others and at most about half can be, some believers must be wrong.
Wrong dimension. The belief is about rank compared with others, not about the size of one's own share. Someone could know their own share exactly and simply underestimate everyone else's.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Some analysts claim that because the price of copper rose sharply last year, worldwide demand for copper must have increased. But a price can rise even when demand stays flat, if supply falls, and last year two of the world's largest copper mines were shut down for months. Last year's price rise is not the evidence of growing demand that the analysts take it to be.
questions.stem: The economist's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that worldwide demand for copper did not increase last year, on the grounds that two major copper mines were shut down
arguing that the general claim on which the analysts rely fails in every case in which the supply of a commodity falls
showing how the evidence that the analysts cite could have come about even if their conclusion were false
establishing that the shutdown of the two mines was the sole cause of the rise in the price of copper last year
pointing out that the analysts' evidence is consistent with an alternative explanation and concluding that the alternative is the more likely one
questions.explanation: The economist shows that the price rise could have come from a fall in supply (the mine closures) even with flat demand, so the rise doesn't establish higher demand; C describes that move. A is the dominant trap: the economist attacks the evidence, not the conclusion, and never says demand didn't rise. E is the near-miss: the economist offers the alternative but never ranks it as more likely. B overstates 'can rise' into 'fails in every case,' and D overstates the closures into the sole cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The price rise does not show that demand for copper increased.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Prices can rise with flat demand if supply falls; two huge mines were shut down for months last year.

breakdown.analysis: What does the economist actually conclude? Read the last sentence carefully: the price rise 'is not the evidence' the analysts think. That's a claim about the evidence, not about demand. The economist attacks the link between evidence and conclusion by showing the evidence (a price rise) could have another source (falling supply). It's like saying: the lawn is wet, but that doesn't prove it rained; the sprinklers were on. Notice that's not the same as saying it didn't rain. We need an answer that says the evidence could exist without the conclusion being true, and nothing stronger. Most students pick (A), because the mine closures look like an argument against higher demand, or (E), because it sounds like a fair summary until 'more likely.'

choices.note: Tempting, because the mine closures seem to cut against rising demand. But the economist never says demand didn't rise. The conclusion is only that the price rise isn't evidence that it did. Attacking the support isn't denying the conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this method: Demand didn't rise, because the mines closed and buyers had nowhere to turn.

choices.note: Too strong. The economist says a price 'can' rise with flat demand if supply falls, not that the analysts' general claim breaks down in every supply drop. One possible exception is enough to sink the inference.
choices.example: Example of this method: Whenever supply falls, a price rise tells you nothing at all about demand, so the analysts' rule never works in such cases.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'How the evidence could have come about' = the supply drop from the mine closures. 'Even if their conclusion were false' = a price rise with flat demand. That's the whole move; the answer claims nothing stronger.
Too strong. The economist says a supply drop could explain the rise, not that it was the only cause; demand may have risen too.
choices.example: Example of this method: Nothing else changed in the market, so the mine closures alone must explain the price rise.

choices.note: Tempting, because the first half is right: the economist does offer an alternative explanation. But the economist never says the supply explanation is more likely than rising demand. The conclusion is only that the evidence doesn't settle it.
choices.example: Example of this method: The price rise could reflect rising demand or the mine closures, and since nothing else in the market changed, the closures are the better bet.

questions.stimulus: Critic: A certain drama prize's committee may consider a play only if that play premiered within the two years before the committee meets. Marrow Lane's first full professional production opened only last spring, so its supporters insist that it is eligible. But the play was first performed three years ago, in a workshop staging before a small invited audience. Therefore, the committee may not consider Marrow Lane.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the critic's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: A play's premiere cannot come after the first time that play is performed before an audience, whether invited or public.
A workshop staging of a play counts as that play's premiere only if the staging is performed before an invited audience.
The committee may consider a play only if that play's first full professional production opened within the two years before the committee meets.
Any play that premiered within the two years before the committee meets may then be considered by the committee.
A workshop staging before an invited audience usually counts as the premiere of the play that is being staged.
questions.explanation: The rule makes a premiere within two years necessary, so the critic needs Marrow Lane's premiere to fall outside that window; A guarantees it, since the play was first performed three years ago and so premiered then or earlier. B is the dominant trap: it reuses the stimulus's own words but gives only a necessary condition for a workshop to be a premiere, so it never establishes that this workshop was one. E is right at the wrong strength ('usually'), and C adds a second requirement that Marrow Lane meets.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The committee may not consider Marrow Lane.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Considered → premiered within the last two years; Marrow Lane's first full production opened last spring (the supporters' point); but it was first performed, in a workshop, three years ago.

breakdown.analysis: When did Marrow Lane premiere: at the workshop three years ago, or at the full production last spring? The supporters assume the latter; the critic assumes the former but never says so. Chain: Considered → premiered within 2 years. Contrapositive: NOT premiered within 2 years → NOT considered. So we need: Marrow Lane did NOT premiere within 2 years. Tie 'premiere' to the first performance: if a premiere can't come after the first performance, Marrow Lane premiered three or more years ago → not within 2 years → not considered. Most students pick (B), because it's about exactly this workshop and invited audience. But 'only if' gives a requirement for a workshop to count, not a guarantee that it does. It's the reversed bridge. (E) is the right idea at the wrong strength.

choices.note: CORRECT. First performance was three years ago, so the premiere was then or earlier: outside the two-year window. Contrapositive of the rule: not considered. The conclusion is locked in.

Tempting, because it describes this exact staging in the stimulus's own words. But 'counts as a premiere only if invited audience' gives a necessary condition. Marrow Lane meets it, but meeting a necessary condition doesn't make the workshop the premiere. This is the reversed bridge.
Tempting, because it adds a requirement. But Marrow Lane's first full production opened last spring, inside the window, so this requirement is met. It can't exclude the play.
This reverses the rule. It tells us which plays may be considered, which can only help a play get in. It can't establish that Marrow Lane is excluded.
Right idea, wrong strength. 'Usually' allows exceptions, and Marrow Lane could be one. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: In a study of people beginning a twelve-week course of therapy, clients who were told at the outset that therapy often feels worse before it feels better were twice as likely to complete the course as clients who were not told this. Yet among the clients who completed the course, those who had been told reported no greater improvement than those who had not. Clearly, then, telling clients what to expect does nothing to increase the number of clients who improve.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that clients who complete a full course of therapy improve more than do clients who drop out partway
treats a mere correlation between being told what to expect and completing therapy as proof that the one causes the other
fails to establish that the clients who were told what to expect actually understood what they were told
confuses the number of clients who complete a course of therapy with the number of clients who improve as a result of therapy
draws a conclusion about an overall total from a comparison confined to a group whose size the practice at issue affected
questions.explanation: Telling clients doubled the number who finished, and the argument compares improvement only among finishers; if finishing helps, more finishers means more people improve in total even though each finisher improves the same. E describes that move abstractly: a conclusion about a total from a comparison inside a group whose size the telling changed. A is the dominant trap because it names the key factor, but the argument does not assume finishers improve more; it ignores that possibility.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Telling clients what to expect does nothing to increase the number of clients who improve.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Told clients were twice as likely to finish; among finishers, told and untold clients reported equal improvement.

breakdown.analysis: Improvement per finisher was the same. Does that mean the number who improve is the same? No. Telling clients doubled the number who finished. If finishing therapy helps, then twice as many finishers means more improved people overall, even though each finisher improves the same amount. The argument compares people inside the finisher group and forgets that the size of that group changed. It's like saying a free shuttle doesn't raise concert attendance because each rider enjoys the show the same as people who drove; the point is that more people got there. We need an answer that says the comparison is limited to a group the telling itself enlarged. Most students pick (A), because it names the key factor, whether finishers improve more. It fails because it's backwards: the argument doesn't assume that; it ignores that possibility. The right answer is abstract ('an overall total,' 'a group whose size the practice at issue affected'), so you have to translate it back: total improvers, the finisher group, telling clients.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the exact factor that matters. But it's backwards. The argument doesn't assume finishers improve more; if they do, the argument fails. The flaw is ignoring that possibility, not assuming it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Clients who finished improved, so finishing therapy must be what made them improve more than dropouts.

choices.note: The argument doesn't rely on this causal claim. Accepting that being told causes completion would actually work against its conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Told clients finished more often, so being told must be what made them finish.

choices.note: So? Whether they understood or not, the study measured the outcomes. This doesn't touch the gap between per-finisher improvement and total improvement.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Clients told about side effects had fewer complaints, so the warning worked (without checking they understood it).

choices.note: Tempting, because it names the two numbers at the heart of the problem. But the argument doesn't confuse them; it keeps them apart. Its mistake is the opposite: it ignores that raising the first number can raise the second.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Twice as many clients finished therapy this year, so twice as many must have been helped by it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Overall total = the number of clients who improve. Comparison confined to a group = told vs. untold among finishers. The practice at issue (telling) doubled that group's size. If finishing helps, more finishers means more improvers, so equal improvement per finisher can't show the total is unchanged.

questions.stimulus: Until two seasons ago, when a certain ski area regraded its beginner slopes, its first-aid staff treated about two hundred skiers a season for injuries suffered on those slopes. Since the regrading, that figure has been about one hundred thirty a season. It follows that the regrading has made the beginner slopes a less dangerous place to ski.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The regrading removed a steep, narrow pitch on which beginning skiers had been hurt more often than anywhere else on those slopes.
Since the regrading, the first-aid staff has treated about as many skiers each season as before for injuries on the area's advanced slopes.
Since the regrading, a clinic in a nearby town has treated more skiers than before for injuries suffered on the area's advanced slopes.
Since the regrading, ski instructors have treated most of the minor injuries their students suffer on the beginner slopes, injuries they formerly sent to the first-aid staff.
Skiers hurt on the beginner slopes are generally less seriously injured than are skiers hurt on the area's steeper slopes.
questions.explanation: The argument measures danger by the first-aid staff's count of beginner-slope injuries. If instructors now handle most minor injuries their students suffer there, many injuries simply stopped reaching first aid, so the count could fall with the slopes no safer (D). C is the near-miss: it diverts injured skiers away from first aid, but for the advanced slopes, so the beginner-slope count is untouched. B, if anything, helps the argument by suggesting skier numbers held steady.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The regrading made the beginner slopes less dangerous.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the regrading, first-aid treatments for beginner-slope injuries fell from about 200 a season to about 130.

breakdown.analysis: Is a lower first-aid count the same as fewer injuries? Only if the count still catches the same share of injuries it used to. The argument treats 'injuries the first-aid staff treated' as a stand-in for 'injuries that happened.' If some injuries now get handled somewhere else, the number can drop while the slopes stay exactly as dangerous. It's like saying a school got healthier because fewer kids visit the nurse, in a year when teachers started handing out bandages in class. Watch the gap between what was measured and what the conclusion is about. Most students pick (B) or (C). (C) mentions treatment outside first aid, which is the right idea, but it's about the advanced slopes. (B) sounds like a control comparison, but steady advanced-slope injuries suggest steady attendance, which helps the argument. The right answer is about ski instructors, which looks like a detail about lessons until you see it changes what the count measures.

choices.note: This strengthens the argument by naming how the regrading could have made the slopes safer. Wrong direction.

Tempting, because it sounds like a control comparison. But steady injuries elsewhere suggest the number of skiers didn't drop, which supports the claim that the regrading made the difference. Wrong direction.
Tempting, because injuries treated outside first aid is exactly the right worry. But this is about advanced-slope injuries. The beginner-slope count the argument relies on is untouched.

CORRECT. Minor beginner-slope injuries that used to show up in the first-aid count are now handled by instructors. So the count can fall from 200 to 130 without any drop in how often skiers get hurt. The evidence no longer measures what the conclusion is about.
True, perhaps, but it doesn't bear on the change. How serious beginner injuries are compared with others says nothing about whether the regrading reduced them.

questions.stimulus: Lionfish, an invasive predator on one Caribbean reef, eat large numbers of young reef fish. Since the regional fisheries agency started paying divers a bounty for each lionfish speared on the reef, divers have killed thousands of lionfish there. So the bounty program must be easing the pressure on the reef's young fish.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Lionfish are the most important predator of young fish on the reef, outranking all of its native predators.
Divers collecting the bounty do not spear any fish other than lionfish while they are diving on the reef.
The reef now holds fewer lionfish than it would have held had the agency never offered the bounty.
Most of the lionfish killed by divers since the bounty began were adults rather than juveniles.
Lionfish killed by divers are replaced more slowly than lionfish that die of natural causes on the reef.
questions.explanation: Killing thousands of lionfish helps young reef fish only if the reef ends up with fewer lionfish than it otherwise would have; C states that counterfactual. Negate it (the reef holds as many lionfish as it would have without the bounty) and predation is unchanged. E is the near-miss: it compares replacement after kills with replacement after natural deaths, which the argument doesn't need. D is tempting because big adults eat more, but killing juveniles also removes predators.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bounty program must be easing predation pressure on the reef's young fish.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lionfish eat many young reef fish; divers have killed thousands of lionfish since the bounty began.

breakdown.analysis: Thousands killed. So what, if thousands more showed up? Invasive species often bounce back fast. If new lionfish moved in or hatched as fast as divers removed them, the reef has as many lionfish as it would have had anyway, and the young fish are no better off. We need an answer that says the kills left the reef with fewer lionfish than it would otherwise have. The right answer is a counterfactual ('than it would have held had...'), which is easy to read past. Most students hunt for something about lionfish being replaced and land on (E), which uses that idea but asks the wrong comparison.

choices.note: Too strong. Lionfish can be the second-biggest predator and removing them still eases pressure.
choices.negation: Lionfish are not the most important predator of young fish on the reef. (Removing them can still help.)

choices.note: Too strong. A diver spearing the occasional grouper doesn't undo the benefit of thousands of dead lionfish.
choices.negation: Some divers spear at least one other kind of fish. (Pressure from lionfish can still be eased.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the reef holds as many lionfish as it would have without the bounty. Then the killing changed nothing about the number of predators, and the pressure hasn't eased. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The reef holds at least as many lionfish as it would have held had the bounty never been offered.

choices.note: Tempting, since big adults eat more. But juveniles eat young fish too, and killing them prevents future predators. Negated, the argument survives.
choices.negation: Most of the lionfish killed were juveniles. (Killing them still removes predators.)

choices.note: Tempting, because replacement is the real issue. But this compares two kinds of deaths. Negate it: killed lionfish are replaced at least as fast as naturally dying ones. Kills could still leave the reef with fewer lionfish than otherwise. Not required.
choices.negation: Lionfish killed by divers are replaced at least as quickly as lionfish that die of natural causes. (The population can still be smaller than it would have been.)

questions.stimulus: Most of the steel bridges in a certain county that were treated with a new anticorrosion coating developed no rust last year. And most of the county's steel bridges were treated with that coating. Thus, most of the county's steel bridges developed no rust last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Most of the members of the town choir who sing tenor also play the piano, and most of the choir's piano players read music fluently. So most of the choir's tenors must read music fluently.
The majority of this orchard's trees bore heavy crops this year. After all, more than half of its trees were pruned last spring, and more than half of the pruned trees bore heavy crops.

Every applicant to the program who submitted a portfolio was granted an interview, and most of the program's applicants submitted a portfolio. So most of the program's applicants were granted an interview.
Most of the town's restaurants that serve breakfast are open on Sundays, and most of the town's restaurants are open on Sundays. So most of the town's restaurants serve breakfast.
Most of the novels on the bookstore's bestseller list were written by first-time authors. So most of the first-time authors whose novels the bookstore sells have written a bestseller.
questions.explanation: The argument combines 'most of the treated bridges were rust-free' with 'most bridges were treated' to get 'most bridges were rust-free,' but most of most can be well under half (60 percent of 60 percent is 36 percent). B makes the same move with pruned trees, stated conclusion-first and with 'more than half' for 'most.' D is the dominant trap: it looks almost identical, but its second premise is about the outcome group rather than the treated group, which is a different error. C is valid, so it can't match.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the county's steel bridges developed no rust last year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most treated bridges developed no rust; most bridges were treated.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most of the Xs that are A are B; most Xs are A; so most Xs are B.

breakdown.analysis: Can 'most of most' give you 'most'? No. Imagine 100 bridges: 60 treated, and 36 of those rust-free (60 percent of the treated). That's only 36 percent of all bridges, plus whatever the 40 untreated bridges did, and they may all have rusted. So the conclusion doesn't follow. The match needs the same two premises: most of a subgroup has the outcome, and the subgroup is most of the whole, concluding most of the whole has the outcome. Watch for disguises: the right answer may lead with its conclusion and say 'more than half' or 'the majority.' Most students pick (D), because its sentence shapes copy the original almost word for word. Look closer: its second premise says most restaurants have the outcome (open Sundays), not the feature, and it concludes the feature. Different error.

choices.note: A different quantifier error: a chain (most tenors play piano, most pianists read music, so most tenors read music). The original's second premise isn't about the outcome group; it says most of the whole has the feature.

CORRECT. Most trees were pruned (most Xs are A); most pruned trees bore heavy crops (most A-Xs are B); so most trees bore heavy crops (most Xs are B). Same 'most of most' error, conclusion moved to the front, 'most' rephrased as 'more than half.'
Valid. 'Every' portfolio submitter was interviewed, and most submitted, so most were interviewed. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.

Tempting, because it looks almost word for word like the original. But its second premise is that most restaurants are open Sundays (the outcome), and it concludes most serve breakfast (the feature). That's a reversal of the original's roles, a different flaw.
Different structure. A single 'most' statement is reversed (most bestsellers by first-timers → most first-timers wrote bestsellers). There's no second premise about how large the subgroup is.
